'''220 yd''': 20.6{{abbr|h|Hand Timed}} (Coral Gables, 1963) '''4 × 100 m''': 39.06{{efn|name=WR}} (Tokyo, 1964) |medaltemplates= {{MedalCountry | the {{USA}} }} {{MedalOlympics}} {{MedalGold|[[1964 Summer Olympics|1964 Tokyo]]|[[Athletics at the 1964 Summer Olympics – Men's 100 metres|100 m]]}} {{MedalGold |[[1964 Summer Olympics|1964 Tokyo]]|[[Athletics at the 1964 Summer Olympics – Men's 4 × 100 metres relay|4 × 100 m relay]]}} }} '''Robert Lee Hayes''' (December 20, 1942 – September 18, 2002), nicknamed "'''Bullet Bob'''", was an American [[sprint (running)|sprinter]] and professional [[American football|football]] player. After winning gold medals at the [[1964 Summer Olympics]], he played as a [[wide receiver|split end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] (for 11 seasons). Hayes is the only athlete to win both an Olympic [[gold medal]] and a [[Super Bowl ring]]. He was a two-sport standout in college in both track and field and [[college football|football]] at [[Florida A&M University]]. Hayes was enshrined in the [[Dallas Cowboys Ring of Honor]] in 2001 and was selected for induction in the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in January 2009. Hayes is the second Olympic gold medalist to be inducted to the Pro Football Hall of Fame, after [[Jim Thorpe]]. Hayes formerly held the Olympic and [[Men's 100 metres world record progression|world record for the 100-meter dash]] with a time of 10.0 seconds, and was part of the team that held the [[Men's 4 × 100 metres relay world record progression|4 × 100 meters world record]] with a time of 39.0 seconds, both set at the 1964 Tokyo Olympics. He also held the world record in the [[60-yard dash|60-yard]], 70-yard, [[100-yard dash|100-yard]], and 220-yard dashes. He was inducted into the [[United States Olympic & Paralympic Hall of Fame|United States Olympic Hall of Fame]].{{cite web |url=https://www.voanews.com/archive/us-olympic-hall-fame-induct-new-members |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200802085543/https://www.voanews.com/archive/us-olympic-hall-fame-induct-new-members |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 2, 2020 |title=US Olympic Hall of Fame to Induct New Members |publisher=[[Voice of America]] |date=October 28, 2009 |access-date=May 11, 2020}} ==Early life== Hayes attended [[Matthew Gilbert High School]] in [[Jacksonville, Florida|Jacksonville]], where he was a halfback on the football team. The 1958 Gilbert High Panthers finished 12–0, winning the [[Florida High School Athletic Association]] black school state championship with a 14–7 victory over [[Dillard High School]] of [[Fort Lauderdale, Florida|Fort Lauderdale]] before more than 11,000 spectators. In times of racial segregation laws, their achievement went basically unnoticed, until 50 years later when they were recognized as one of the best teams in [[Florida High School Athletic Association]] (FHSAA) history. ==College career== A highly recruited athlete, Hayes accepted a football scholarship from [[Florida A&M University]], a [[historically black colleges and universities|historically black college]], where he excelled in track and field. In 1962, the [[University of Miami]] invited him to a meet on their campus, where he tied the world record of 9.2 seconds in the [[100-yard dash]], which had been set by [[Frank Budd]] of [[Villanova University]] the previous year. He also was the first person to break six seconds in the 60-yard dash with his indoor world record of 5.9 seconds. In 1963, he broke the [[100-yard dash]] record with a time of 9.1 seconds,{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=OxdZAAAAIBAJ&sjid=FOMDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6504%2C4186516 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title=100-yard dash record shaved to 9.1 by Hayes |date=June 22, 1963 |page=1B}}{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=UERjAAAAIBAJ&sjid=PHQNAAAAIBAJ&pg=6555%2C3607594 |work=Wilmington Morning Star |location=North Carolina |agency=UPI |title=Hayes shatters world record |date=June 22, 1963 |page=6}} a mark that would not be broken for eleven years until [[Ivory Crockett]] ran a 9.0 in 1974. The same year, Hayes set the world best for 200 meters (20.5 seconds, although the time was never ratified) and ran the 220-yard dash in a time of 20.6 seconds (while running into an {{convert|8|mph|m/s|abbr=on}} wind). He was selected to represent the United States in the [[1964 Summer Olympics]] in Tokyo. His football coach [[Jake Gaither]] was not very high on giving Hayes time to train, which caused then president [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] to call him and insist he allow Hayes time off and to keep him healthy.{{cite news| last=Deford | first=Frank | url=https://www.si.com/vault/2001/08/06/308496/time-bandits-maurice-greene-is-the-latest-holder-of-the-grand-and-curious-title-worlds-fastest-human-bestowed-on-men-who-have-stolen-fractions-of-seconds-from-the-100-meter-record | title=Time Bandits Maurice Greene is the latest holder of the grand and curious title World's Fastest Human | access-date=February 19, 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160611181146/http://www.si.com/vault/2001/08/06/308496/time-bandits-maurice-greene-is-the-latest-holder-of-the-grand-and-curious-title-worlds-fastest-human-bestowed-on-men-who-have-stolen-fractions-of-seconds-from-the-100-meter-record | archive-date=June 11, 2016 | url-status=dead | work=si.com}} Hayes' running form was considered unusual for a sprinter due to his long strides and large frame. He was the AAU 100-yard dash champion three years running, from 1962 to 1964, and in 1964 was the NCAA champion in the 200-meter dash. He missed part of his senior year because of his Olympic bid for the gold medal. In 1976, he was inducted into the inaugural class of the Florida A&M University Sports Hall of Fame. In 1996, he was inducted into the [[Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference]] Hall of Fame. In 2011, he was inducted into the [[Black College Football Hall of Fame]]. ==Olympics== [[File:Bob Hayes 1964.jpg|thumb|220px|Hayes at the 1964 Olympics]] [[File:FAMU athlete Robert Hayes practices running on the track.jpg|thumb|right|170px|At FAMU in 1962]] At the [[1964 Summer Olympics]], in Tokyo, Hayes won the 100 m and in doing so tied the then [[Men's 100 metres world record progression|world record in the 100 m]] with a time of 10.0 seconds. Until the Tokyo Olympics, world records were measured by officials with stopwatches, measured to the nearest tenth of a second; [[Fully automatic time|fully automatic timing]] was used in Tokyo, but the times were recorded as "hand-timed" by subtracting 0.05 seconds from the automatic time and rounding to the nearest tenth of a second. Officials with stopwatches had measured Hayes' time to be 9.9 seconds, but his automatically-timed 10.06 seconds was converted to 10.0 seconds.[https://web.archive.org/web/20131113125002/http://www.trackandfieldnews.com/discussion/viewtopic.php?f=5&t=52318 revisionist history: men's 100 WR]. Track and Field News. November 1, 2013 Hayes ran in lane 1 which had been used for the 20 km racewalk the previous day and this badly damaged the cinder track, and ran in borrowed spikes because one of his shoes had been kicked under the bed when he was playing with some friends and he didn't realize until he got there.Hayes, Bob (1992) ''Run, Bullet, Run: The Rise, Fall, and Recovery of Bob Hayes''. New York: Harper & Row. {{ISBN|0060182008}}. Hayes won another gold medal in the 4 × 100-meter relay, setting a new world record at 39.06 seconds with team-mates [[Paul Drayton (athlete)|Paul Drayton]], [[Gerry Ashworth]], and [[Richard Stebbins]].{{cite Sports-Reference |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/athletes/ha/bob-hayes-1.html |title=Bob Hayes |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417094344/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/athletes/ha/bob-hayes-1.html |archive-date=April 17, 2020}} Hayes ran the anchor leg in a come-from-behind win for the US team. Hand-timed between 8.5 and 8.9 seconds, his relay leg is one of the [[Anchor leg#All-time top 10 (men)|fastest in history]].[https://web.archive.org/web/20121113200001/http://sports.espn.go.com/oly/summer08/fanguide/athlete?athlete=5325 Bob Hayes – Olympics Athletes – 2008 Summer Olympics – Beijing, China – ESPN]. Sports.espn.go.com. [[Jocelyn Delecour]], France's anchor leg runner, famously said to [[Paul Drayton (athlete)|Paul Drayton]] before the relay final that, "You can't win, all you have is Bob Hayes." Drayton was able to reply afterwards, "That's all we need." The race was also Hayes' last as a track and field athlete, as he permanently switched to football after it, aged only 21.{{YouTube|mh-YLy_wnrc|See the race}} In some of the first meets to be timed with experimental [[Fully automatic time|fully automatic timing]], Hayes was the first man to break the ten-second barrier for the 100 meters, albeit with a 5.3 m/s [[wind assistance]] in the semi-finals of the 1964 Olympics. His time was recorded at 9.91 seconds. [[Jim Hines]] officially broke 10 seconds at the high altitude of Mexico City, Mexico in 1968 with a wind-legal 9.95s which stood as the world record for almost 15 years. Hayes' low-altitude record was equaled by [[Hasely Crawford]] in 1976 and broken by [[Carl Lewis]] in 1984.[http://run-down.com/guests/jc_bobhayes.php JC Bob Hayes]. Run-down.com. Retrieved on May 30, 2015. ==Professional football career== ===Dallas Cowboys=== The [[Dallas Cowboys]] selected Hayes in the seventh round (88th overall) of the [[1964 NFL draft]] with a future draft pick, which allowed the team to draft him before his college eligibility was over, taking a chance that the Olympic sprinter with unrefined football skills could excel as a [[wide receiver]].[https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2202&dat=19641209&id=PyEmAAAAIBAJ&sjid=CP4FAAAAIBAJ&pg=2456,1931474 Cowboys and Giants Sign 2 Speedsters]. Gettysburg Times. December 9, 1964 Hayes wore No. 22 with the Cowboys, which would later be worn by [[running back]] [[Emmitt Smith]]. He was also selected by the [[Denver Broncos]] in the 14th round (105th overall) of the [[1964 American Football League draft|1964 AFL draft]] as a future selection. Hayes has been credited by many with forcing the NFL to develop a [[zone defense]] and the [[bump and run coverage|bump and run]] to attempt to contain him.[http://www.profootballhof.com/enshrinement/story.jsp?story_id=3095 Enshrinement » Class of 2009 announced] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090203071341/http://www.profootballhof.com/enshrinement/story.jsp?story_id=3095 |date=February 3, 2009 }}. Profootballhof.com. Retrieved on May 30, 2015. Hayes' first two seasons were successful, during which he led the NFL both times in receiving touchdowns with 12 and 13 touchdowns, respectively.{{cite web|last=Rank|first=Adam|url=http://www.nfl.com/photoessays/0ap2000000324888/NFL-players-from-historically-black-colleges|title=NFL players from historically black colleges|publisher=[[National Football League]]|date=February 10, 2014|access-date=February 27, 2014}} In 1966 Hayes caught six passes for 195 yards against the [[New York Giants]] at the [[Cotton Bowl (stadium)|Cotton Bowl]]. Later, in the [[Dallas Cowboys]]-[[Washington Commanders|Washington Redskins]] match-up, Hayes caught nine passes for 246 yards (a franchise record until [[Miles Austin]] broke it with a 250-yard performance on October 11, 2009, against the [[Kansas City Chiefs]]). Hayes' speed forced other teams to go to a zone since no single player could keep up with him. Spreading the defense out in hopes of containing Hayes allowed the Cowboys' talented running game to flourish, rushers [[Don Perkins]], [[Calvin Hill]], [[Walt Garrison]] and [[Duane Thomas]] taking advantage of the diminished coverage at the line of scrimmage. In the 1967 season, Hayes led the NFL in punt return yards, and went on to set an NFL playoff record with 141 punt return yards in Dallas' 52-14 win over the [[Cleveland Browns]]. Hayes also caught 5 passes for 145 yards in that game, including an 86-yard touchdown catch. Hayes is also known for two events, both involving the NFL championship games in [[1966 NFL Championship Game|1966]] and [[1967 NFL Championship Game|1967]] against the [[Green Bay Packers]]. In the 1966 game, on the last meaningful play of the game, Hayes missed an assignment of blocking linebacker [[Dave Robinson (American football)|Dave Robinson]], which resulted in [[Don Meredith]] nearly being sacked by Robinson and as a result throwing a desperation pass into the end zone that was intercepted by [[Tom Brown (safety)|Tom Brown]]. In the 1967 NFL championship, the "Ice Bowl" played on New Year's Eve, 1967, Hayes was alleged to have inadvertently disclosed whether the upcoming play was a pass or run because on running plays he kept his hands inside his pants to keep them warm and the Green Bay defense knew they didn't need to cover him.{{cite web| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/playoffs/2014/story/_/id/12127344/nfl-chilling-recollection-classic-ice-bowl | title=A chilling recollection of 'Ice Bowl' | date=January 7, 2015 | access-date=February 19, 2016}} On July 17, 1975, he was traded to the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in exchange for a third round draft choice (#73-[[Duke Fergerson]]).{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2202&dat=19750718&id=ALslAAAAIBAJ&pg=1047,3651557&hl=es | title=Bob Hayes, Traded By Dallas To San Francisco | access-date=February 19, 2016}} ===San Francisco 49ers=== In the [[1975 NFL season|1975 season]] with the [[1975 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]], Hayes teamed up with [[Gene Washington (American football, born 1947)|Gene Washington]] in the starting lineup. After not playing up to expectations in the first five games, he was waived on October 22 to make room for [[wide receiver]] [[Terry Beasley]].{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2457&dat=19751023&id=MRQ9AAAAIBAJ&pg=5030,3103651&hl=es |work=Bangor Daily News |location=Maine |agency=UPI |title=San Francisco waives Bob Hayes |date=October 23, 1975 |page=13 |access-date=February 19, 2016}}{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Ti8PAAAAIBAJ&sjid=hIUDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6064%2C4021842 |work=Victoria Advocate |location=Texas |agency=Associated Press |title=49ers waive Hayes |date=October 23, 1975 |page=2B}} ===Multiple offensive threat=== In addition to receiving, Hayes returned punts for the Cowboys and was the NFL's leading [[Return specialist#Punt returner|punt returner]] in 1968 with a 20.8 yards per return average and two touchdowns, including a 90 yarder against the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. He was named to the [[Pro Bowl]] three times and First-team All-Pro twice and Second-team All-Pro twice. He helped Dallas win five Eastern Conference titles, two NFC titles, played in two Super Bowls, and was instrumental in Dallas' first-ever Super Bowl victory after the 1971 season, making Hayes the only person to win both an Olympic [[gold medal]] and a [[Super Bowl#Super Bowl winners|Super Bowl ring]]. Later in his career, as defenses improved playing zone and the bump and run was refined, Hayes' value was as a decoy rather than a deep threat. ===Cowboy records=== Hayes was the second player (after [[Frank Clarke (American football)|Franklin Clarke]]) in the history of the [[Dallas Cowboys]] franchise to surpass 1,000 yards (ground or air) in a single season, and he did that in his rookie year by finishing with 1,003 yards. Also during his rookie year, he led the team with 46 receptions and set franchise records for total [[touchdowns]] (13) and total receiving touchdowns (12). He finished his 11-year career with 371 receptions for 7,414 yards and 71 touchdowns, giving him an impressive 20 yards per catch average (his yards per catch average remains a franchise record, while his touchdown reception record stood until 2017, when it was broken by [[Dez Bryant]].) He also rushed for 68 yards on 24 carries and two touchdowns, gained 581 yards on 23 kickoff returns, and returned 104 punts for 1,158 yards and three touchdowns. In [[1965 NFL season|1965]] he also started a streak ([[1965 NFL season|1965]]–[[1966 NFL season|1966]]) of seven consecutive games with at least a [[touchdown]] catch, which still stands as a Cowboys record shared with [[Frank Clarke (American football)|Franklin Clarke]] ([[1961 NFL season|1961]]–[[1962 NFL season|1962]]), [[Terrell Owens]] ([[2007 NFL season|2007]]) and [[Dez Bryant]] ([[2012 NFL season|2012]]). His 7,295 receiving yards are the sixth-most in [[Dallas Cowboys]] history. Hayes holds ten regular-season receiving records, four punt return records, and 22 overall franchise records, making him one of the greatest receivers to ever play for the Cowboys. In 2004, he was named to the [[Professional Football Researchers Association]] Hall of Very Good in the association's second HOVG class.{{cite web |url=http://www.profootballresearchers.org/hall-of-very-good-2004.htm |title=Hall of Very Good |access-date=July 13, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161005051004/http://www.profootballresearchers.org/hall-of-very-good-2004.htm |archive-date=October 5, 2016 |url-status=dead }} ==NFL career statistics== {| class="wikitable" ! colspan="2"| Legend |- | style="background:#afe6ba; width:3em;"| | Won the [[Super Bowl]] |- | style="background:#cfecec; width:3em;"| | Led the league |- | '''Bold''' | Career high |} ===Regular season=== {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center;" |- ! rowspan="2"| Year ! rowspan="2"| Team ! colspan="2"| Games ! colspan="5"| Receiving ! colspan="5"| Rushing ! colspan="5"| Kick returns ! colspan="5"| Punt returns |- ! He continued to battle drug and alcohol problems and went to rehab on three occasions. Hayes moved back to Jacksonville in the mid-1990s to live with his parents and went back to Florida A&M and completed work on his bachelor's degree in elementary education in 1994. He spent much of his time speaking out against drug abuse and urging athletes to work towards their college degree.{{Cite web |last=Raynor |first=Brett |title=The story of Jacksonville's Bullet Bob Hayes |url=https://www.jacksonville.com/story/opinion/columns/mike-clark/2018/11/11/uncovering-our-history-jacksonvilles-incomparable-bob-hayes/8405336007/ |access-date=February 13, 2026 |website=The Florida Times-Union |language=en-US}}{{Cite news |date=March 23, 1979 |title=Hayes: 5 Years In Prison |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1979/03/23/archives/hayes-5-years-in-prison.html |access-date=February 13, 2026 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}{{Cite web |title=ESPN Classic - Hayes was golden receiver for Cowboys |url=https://www.espn.com/classic/obit/s/2001/0427/1187536.html |access-date=February 13, 2026 |website=www.espn.com}} ==Death== On September 18, 2002, Hayes died in his hometown of Jacksonville of [[kidney]] failure, after battling [[prostate cancer]] and [[liver]] ailments."Ex-Olympic star, Cowboy Hayes dies," AP, as reported by [https://web.archive.org/web/20021003225719/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/football/news/2002/09/19/hayes_obit_ap/ ''CNNSI.com,'' September 19, 2002]. [retrieved September 11, 2011] ==Pro Football Hall of Fame== ===2004 controversy=== Hayes was close to being inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2004, but was denied the opportunity in the final round of decision-making. The decision was marred by controversy, with many claiming that the Hall of Fame Senior Selection Committee had a bias against members of the Dallas Cowboys and other NFL teams.{{cite web| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=1726974 | title=Zimmerman: Hayes deserved to get in | date=February 4, 2004 | access-date=February 19, 2016}} Others believe Hayes' legal and drug use issues marred his chances.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=gpUyAAAAIBAJ&sjid=NOcFAAAAIBAJ&pg=6681%2C4521393 |work=Lawrence Daily Journal-World |location=Kansas |agency=Associated Press |title=Downfall of ex-Cowboy star Hayes: Last week they sprayed him for lice |date=April 22, 1979 |page=5B}}{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=8PtPAAAAIBAJ&sjid=zQgEAAAAIBAJ&hl=es&pg=1980%2C1036472 |work=Ocala Star-Banner |location=Florida |last=Word |first=Ron |agency=Associated Press |title='Bullet' Bob Hayes dies of kidney failure |date=September 20, 2002 |page=1C}} Shortly after the announcement of the new 2004 Hall of Fame members, long-time ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' writer [[Paul Zimmerman (sportswriter)|Paul Zimmerman]] resigned from the Selection Committee in protest of the decision to leave Hayes out of the Hall. Zimmerman eventually returned as a Hall of Fame voter.[http://www.thefootballsearchengine.com/JimMarshall/HOFvoters/ Pro Football Hall of Fame Voters]. Thefootballsearchengine.com. Retrieved on May 30, 2015. ===2009 induction=== On August 27, 2008, Hayes was named as one of two senior candidates for the 2009 Hall of Fame election.[http://www.profootballhof.com/enshrinement/story.jsp?story_id=2816 Enshrinement » Class of '09 senior candidates] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080903085641/http://www.profootballhof.com/enshrinement/story.jsp?story_id=2816 |date=September 3, 2008}}. Profootballhof.com. Retrieved on May 30, 2015. On Saturday, January 31, 2009, he was selected as a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame's Class of 2009. The next day Lucille Hester, who claimed to be Hayes's sister,{{Cite web|last=Frenette|first=Gene|title=Hayes' Hall saga now soap opera|url=https://www.jacksonville.com/article/20090204/news/801240033|access-date=October 17, 2020|website=The Florida Times-Union|language=en|archive-date=October 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201019030827/https://www.jacksonville.com/article/20090204/news/801240033|url-status=dead}} released a letter she said he had drafted three years before he died, on October 29, 1999, in case he did not live to see his induction. Its full text read:
You know I am not sure I am going to be around if I get into the Pro Football Hall of Fame so you must read this for me, I am not sure, I guess I am feeling sorry for myself at this time but you must remember everything I want you to do and say. Mother said you would do what I want because you always did. So read this for me. I would like to thank everyone who supported me to get into the NFL Hall of Fame, the Dallas Cowboys organization, all of my team mates and everyone who played for the Cowboys, (thank the San Francisco 49rs {{sic}} too). Thank the fans all around the country and the world, thank the committee who voted for me and also the ones who may did not vote for me, thank Mother and my family, thank Roger Stauback {{sic}} and tell all my teammates I love them dearly. Thank the Pro Football Hall of Fame, all the NFL teams and players, Florida A&M University, thank everyone who went to Mathew {{sic}} Gilbert High School, thank everyone in Jacksonville and Florida and everyone especially on the East Side of Jacksonville. Thank everyone in the City of Dallas and in Texas and just thank everyone in the whole world. I love you all.
Delivered by Hester in front of hundreds and a national cable television audience, the moment was described as "... one of the most compelling and touching scenes the Hall of Fame has seen."{{cite news| url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/2009/01/31/2009-01-31_late_receiver_bob_hayes_sister_reads_tha-2.html | location=New York | work=Daily News | title=Late receiver Bob Hayes' sister reads thank-you letter to Hall of Fame | first=Gary | last=Myers | date=January 31, 2009}} Shortly after, it was discovered that the supposedly signed letter was printed in the [[Calibri]] font, which was not released to the public until five years after Hayes' death.{{cite news |last1=Townsend |first1=Brad |title=Letter purportedly from former Dallas Cowboy Hayes under more scrutiny |url=http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/dws/spt/stories/020509dnspocowhayes.9a30e7.html |access-date=November 26, 2024 |work=[[The Dallas Morning News]] |date=February 5, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100116001003/http://www.dallasnews.com/sharedcontent/dws/spt/stories/020509dnspocowhayes.9a30e7.html |archive-date=January 16, 2010}} Some family members disputed Lucille Hester's claim to be related to Bob, and took steps to ensure she was not part of the Hall of Fame ceremony.[http://dal.scout.com/2/835595.html Dallas Cowboys NFL Football Front Page] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090204052000/http://dal.scout.com/2/835595.html |date=February 4, 2009 }}. Dal.scout.com (May 5, 2015). Retrieved on May 30, 2015.Fisher, Mike. [https://web.archive.org/web/20090418163010/http://dallasbasketball.com/fullColumn.php?id=1291 Is Bob Hayes' 'Sister' Conning The Cowboys, The Hall Of Fame And The NFL?] Dallas Basketball On August 8, 2009, Hayes was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. [[Roger Staubach]], Hayes' Dallas Cowboy teammate, along with Hayes' son Bob Hayes Jr., unveiled the bust, which was sculpted by [[Scott Myers]]. On hand were six members of Bob's Gilbert High School championship team.[https://archive.today/20120904025047/http://www.jacksonville.com/sports/columnists/gene_frenette/2009-08-09/story/bob_hayes_finally_crosses_finish_line_in_canton Bob Hayes finally crosses finish line in Canton]. jacksonville.com. '''Robert Allen Griese''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɡ|r|iː|s|i}} {{respell|GREE|see}}; born February 3, 1945) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] for 14 seasons with the [[Miami Dolphins]] of the [[American Football League]] (AFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL). He earned [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors playing [[college football]] for the [[Purdue Boilermakers football|Purdue Boilermakers]] before being selected by the Dolphins of the AFL in the [[1967 NFL/AFL draft]].

Widely regarded as one of the greatest quarterbacks of the 1970s, Griese led the Dolphins to a then record three consecutive [[Super Bowl]] appearances,<ref name=hofhistory>{{cite web |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/teams/miami-dolphins/team-history/ |title=Miami Dolphins Team History |website=profootballhof.com |access-date=March 17, 2020 |archive-date=June 10, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200610125659/https://www.profootballhof.com/teams/miami-dolphins/team-history/ |url-status=live }}</ref> including two Super Bowl victories in [[Super Bowl VII|VII]] and [[Super Bowl VIII|VIII]],<ref>{{cite web | last=Frank | first=Vincent | title=Ranking the best NFL quarterbacks of the 1970s | website=Sportsnaut | date=February 23, 2021 | url=https://sportsnaut.com/nfl/ranking-the-best-nfl-quarterbacks-of-the-1970s/ | access-date=May 18, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.foxsports.com/stories/nfl/the-top-10-nfl-quarterbacks-of-the-1970s | title=The top 10 NFL quarterbacks of the 1970s | Fox Sports }}</ref> the first of which capped off [[1972 Miami Dolphins season|Miami's undefeated and untied 1972 season]], the only such season in NFL history. Griese was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] and the [[Indiana Football Hall of Fame]] in 1984,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cfbhall.com/about/inductees/ |title=College Football Hall of Fame Inductees |access-date=March 10, 2020 |archive-date=August 7, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160807014549/http://www.cfbhall.com/inductees/?player=0732&tt=1414537148 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.indiana-football.org/?q=node/334 |title=Indiana Football Hall of Fame |access-date=March 10, 2020 |archive-date=August 21, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180821093918/http://www.indiana-football.org/?q=node%2F334 |url-status=live }}</ref> and the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 1990.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/#p=GrieseBob |title=Bob Griese |website=profootballhof.com |access-date=March 10, 2020 |archive-date=March 29, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200329032819/https://www.profootballhof.com/players/#p=GrieseBob |url-status=live }}</ref> He later worked as a television commentator, calling NFL games for [[NBC Sports]] and [[college football]] for [[ESPN]] and [[ABC Sports]]. Griese is one of three quarterbacks from Purdue to win the Super Bowl (along with [[Len Dawson]] and [[Drew Brees]]).<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.newsday.com/sports/football/super-bowl/super-bowl-winning-quarterbacks-by-college-team-1.11426285 |title=Super Bowl champion QBs by alma mater |website=newsday.com |date=February 2, 2020 |access-date=March 10, 2020 |archive-date=February 4, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200204175711/https://www.newsday.com/sports/football/super-bowl/super-bowl-winning-quarterbacks-by-college-team-1.11426285 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Early life==
Griese was born in [[Evansville, Indiana]], to Ida (Ulrich) and Sylverious "Slick" Griese. Slick owned a plumbing company in Evansville and died in 1955 when he was ten years old. He primarily played baseball and excelled as a pitcher. He also played basketball and football at Evansville's [[Rex Mundi High School]], and earned 12 varsity letters for the Monarchs.

===Baseball===
In the summer of 1963, Griese led his [[American Legion Baseball]] team, Funkhouser Post #8 of [[Evansville, Indiana]], to the American Legion Baseball World Series as the Region 5 champion. His team did not reach the finals, as the Arthur L. Peterson Post of [[Long Beach, California]], won the title.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.legion.org/documents/baseball/national_champions.pdf |title=American Legion Baseball National Champions – 1926 to 2014 |website=legion.org |access-date=January 7, 2020 |archive-date=May 16, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190516230954/https://www.legion.org/documents/baseball/national_champions.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Basketball===
He led the basketball team to the No. 1 ranking in Indiana during the 1962–63 season and a record of 19–3. He scored 900 points in his high school career and while being named '''All-Sectional''', he could not lead the Monarchs past Evansville Bosse in the highly competitive Evansville IHSAA Sectional.<ref name="local.evpl.org">{{cite news |url=http://local.evpl.org/views/viewimage.asp?ID=712938 |title=Coaching Doesn't Intrigue Bob Griese |date=April 27, 1963 |publisher=The Evansville Press |author=Tom Tuley |access-date=March 10, 2020 |archive-date=December 14, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131214013352/http://local.evpl.org/views/viewimage.asp?ID=712938 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Football===
The Monarchs were 15–5 during his Junior (9–1) and Senior (6–4) seasons, as he was named 1st Team All-City for three seasons.<ref name="local.evpl.org"/> After being recruited by several colleges for football, Bob chose [[Purdue University]], where he majored in management (Krannert School of Management) and became a three-sport star.<ref>(cited from ''Undefeated'', by Bob Griese, copyright 2000)</ref>

==College career==
[[File:Bob Griese 1966.jpg|thumb|left|175px|Griese from 1967 Purdue yearbook]]
While at Purdue, Griese became a member of [[Sigma Chi]] fraternity.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://members.sigmachi.org/Shared_Content/Custom/Fraternity/Alumni_Services/Awards/Significant_Sigs.aspx?field_oc_ss_last_initial_value=All&field_hp_company_value=All&field_hp_univ_preferred_value=All&field_hp_province_description_value=All&field_hp_state_province_value=All&page=5 |title=Significant Sig Recipients |access-date=January 8, 2020 |publisher=[[Sigma Chi]] |website=sigmachi.org |archive-date=May 2, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502031307/https://members.sigmachi.org//Shared_Content/Custom/Fraternity/Alumni_Services/Awards/Significant_Sigs.aspx?field_oc_ss_last_initial_value=All&field_hp_company_value=All&field_hp_univ_preferred_value=All&field_hp_province_description_value=All&field_hp_state_province_value=All&page=5 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Griese pitched for the Purdue baseball team, going 12–1 one season, played guard on the Purdue basketball team, and played quarterback, kicker, and punter for the Purdue football team.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.courierpress.com/story/sports/2019/01/21/griese-mattingly-share-spotlight-among-local-legends/2603505002/ |title=Griese, Mattingly set standard among Evansville male athletes |last=Engelhardt |first=Gordon |date=January 21, 2019 |newspaper=Evansville Courier & Press |access-date=April 1, 2020 |archive-date=August 11, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200811033136/https://www.courierpress.com/story/sports/2019/01/21/griese-mattingly-share-spotlight-among-local-legends/2603505002/ |url-status=live }}</ref> There are at least four football games in which Griese was in some way responsible for all of Purdue's points.<ref>{{cite news |title=Purdue Blanks Out-Manned Ohio U., 17–0 |newspaper=The Terre Haute Tribune |date=September 27, 1964 |page=50 |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8428107/purdue_blanks_outmanned_ohio_u_170/ |via=Newspapers.com |access-date=March 10, 2020 |archive-date=October 29, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191029152043/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/8428107/purdue_blanks_outmanned_ohio_u_170/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Griese Lifts Purdue Past Michigan, 17–15 |newspaper=Detroit Free Press |author=Jack Saylor |date=October 17, 1965 |pages=1C, 3C |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/38845018/griese_lifts_purdue_past_michigan_1715/ |via=Newspapers.com |access-date=March 10, 2020 |archive-date=November 11, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191111233747/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/38845018/griese_lifts_purdue_past_michigan_1715/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

As of the beginning of the 2016 NCAA football season, Griese ranks #10 in all-time scoring at Purdue;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://purduesports.com/sports/2018/5/17/sports-m-footbl-spec-rel-legends-griese-html.aspx |title=Legends of Purdue Football: Bob Griese |website=purduesports.com |access-date=January 7, 2020 |archive-date=May 2, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502031313/https://purduesports.com/sports/2018/5/17/sports-m-footbl-spec-rel-legends-griese-html.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref> #5 in scoring among non-kickers and #4 among kickers. Griese's passing skills greatly improved under the tutelage of head coach [[Jack Mollenkopf]] and quarterback coach [[Bob DeMoss]].

In his junior year at Purdue in a game against the top-ranked [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame]], Griese completed 19 of 22 passes as he led the Boilermakers to an upset win.<ref>{{College Football HoF|id=1868}}</ref>

Griese was a two-time All-American at Purdue, finishing at No. 8 in the 1965 [[Heisman Trophy]] race and was the runner-up to [[Steve Spurrier]] for the 1966 [[Heisman Trophy]]. Purdue finished second in the Big Ten in 1966, and he led the school's first appearance in the [[Rose Bowl Game|Rose Bowl]], where they defeated [[University of Southern California|USC]] 14–13. He was inducted into the Rose Bowl Hall of Fame in 1992.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tournamentofroses.com/the-rose-bowl-game/history/rose-bowl-hall-of-fame/history |title=The Rose Bowl Game® presented by VIZIO |access-date=December 10, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101208024631/http://www.tournamentofroses.com/the-rose-bowl-game/history/rose-bowl-hall-of-fame/history |archive-date=December 8, 2010 }}</ref> He also won the [[Big Ten Medal of Honor]] for excellence in athletics and academics.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://local.evpl.org/views/viewimage.asp?ID=712514 |title=Bob Griese Earns Final Honor for Football, Scholastic Abilities |date=June 5, 1967 |access-date=March 10, 2020 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304084115/http://local.evpl.org/views/viewimage.asp?ID=712514 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Griese's achievements during his college career earned him induction into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 1984. Purdue does not have a practice of [[Retired number|retiring]] jersey numbers, but he was inducted as an inaugural member of the Purdue Intercollegiate Athletic Hall of Fame in 1994.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://purduesports.com/sports/2018/5/17/school-bio-pur-hallfame-html.aspx |title=Purdue Intercollegiate Athletics Hall of Fame |access-date=March 10, 2020 |archive-date=November 7, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191107021334/https://purduesports.com/sports/2018/5/17/school-bio-pur-hallfame-html.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref>

On December 11, 2014, the [[Big Ten Network]] included Griese on "The Mount Rushmore of [[Purdue football program|Purdue Football]]", as chosen by online fan voting. Griese was joined in the honor by [[Drew Brees]], [[Rod Woodson]], and [[Leroy Keyes]].

==Professional career==

===1967–1969===
Griese was selected by the AFL's [[Miami Dolphins]] as the fourth player in the [[1967 NFL draft|1967 Common Draft]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1967/draft.htm |title=1967 NFL Draft |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=March 17, 2020 |archive-date=October 23, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181023155900/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1967/draft.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Griese threw for 2,005 yards and 15 touchdowns his rookie year.

Griese was an [[American Football League All-Star games|AFL All-Star]] his first two years with the Dolphins, and earned AFL All-Star or AFC-NFC Pro Bowl honors in six additional seasons.<ref name=griesepfr>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GrieBo00.htm |title=Bob Griese |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=March 17, 2020 |archive-date=May 2, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502031323/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GrieBo00.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> While he never put up huge numbers, his leadership played an important role in helping the Dolphins compete in three consecutive [[Super Bowl]]s, winning the latter two contests.<ref name=hofhistory/>

Griese started the season as the team's second-string quarterback behind [[John Stofa]]. When Stofa broke his ankle in the first quarter of the first game of the 1967 season, Griese stepped in and led the Dolphins to a 35–21 victory against the [[Denver Broncos]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1967_AFL/games.htm |title=1967 AFL Weekly League Schedule |website= pro-football-reference.com |access-date=March 17, 2020 |archive-date=November 8, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201108133721/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1967_AFL/games.htm |url-status= live }}</ref> The 1967, 1968, and 1969 seasons were tough for the expansion Dolphins. After a difficult 1969 season that was worse than the 1968 season, coach [[George Wilson (football coach)|George Wilson]] was fired.

===1970–1976===
Dolphins owner [[Joe Robbie]] brought in [[Don Shula]] from the Baltimore Colts in 1970,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.miamidolphins.com/news/in-my-own-words-50-years-later-dolphins-hire-don-shula |title=In My Own Words 50 Years Later: Dolphins Hire Don Shula |author=Don Shula |date=February 18, 2020 |access-date=March 11, 2020 |archive-date=February 19, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200219174511/https://www.miamidolphins.com/news/in-my-own-words-50-years-later-dolphins-hire-don-shula |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |magazine=Sports Illustrated |url=http://vault.sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1084265/index.htm |title=The Rosenbloom-Robbie Bowl |author=Jack Olsen |date=November 9, 1970 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080725123948/http://vault.sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1084265/index.htm |archive-date=July 25, 2008 |url-status=dead |access-date=March 11, 2020}}</ref> and the team's personality and fortunes turned quickly. The Dolphins found a new discipline, and learned what it took to become a winning team. They went from a 3–10–1 record in 1969 to 10–4 in 1970, making the playoffs.<ref name=lambwfr>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=gqlRAAAAIBAJ&pg=6250%2C6363585 |work=Milwaukee Sentinel |agency=UPI |title=Lamonica's 'bomb' wins for Raiders |date=December 28, 1970 |page=1, part 2 }}{{Dead link|date=October 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref name=ldslsld>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=DlszAAAAIBAJ&pg=2710%2C7809465 |work=Lodi News-Sentinel |location=California |agency=UPI |title=Oakland slips, slides past Dolphin defense |date=December 28, 1970 |page=22 |access-date=October 6, 2020 |archive-date=May 2, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502031308/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=DlszAAAAIBAJ&pg=2710%2C7809465 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=sivrtsac>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.si.com/vault/1971/01/04/554208/rushing-to-stake-a-claim |magazine=Sports Illustrated |last=Maule |first=Tex |author-link=Tex Maule |title=Rushing to stake a claim |date=January 4, 1971 |page=10 |access-date=March 17, 2020 |archive-date=November 6, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191106204059/https://www.si.com/vault/1971/01/04/554208/rushing-to-stake-a-claim |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 1971, the Dolphins made it to the Super Bowl,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197201160dal.htm |title=Super Bowl VI – Miami Dolphins vs. Dallas Cowboys – January 16th, 1972 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=March 17, 2020 |archive-date=August 7, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190807124648/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197201160dal.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> losing 24–3 to the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. Griese was named the 1971 Newspaper Enterprise Association NFL Most Valuable Player award,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/awards/newspaper-entertainment-mvp.htm |title=The Newspaper Enterprise Association NFL Most Valuable Player Winners |website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |access-date=March 11, 2020 |archive-date=June 10, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160610023941/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/awards/newspaper-entertainment-mvp.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> and won the [[Jim Thorpe Trophy]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Bob Griese Gets Thorpe Trophy As Top Player |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2202&dat=19720105&id=YH9bAAAAIBAJ&pg=6950,173400&hl=en |access-date=March 11, 2020 |work=Gettysburg Times |agency=Associated Press |date=January 5, 1972 |page=4 |archive-date=May 2, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210502031307/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2202&dat=19720105&id=YH9bAAAAIBAJ&pg=6950%2C173400&hl=en |url-status=live }}</ref>

The 1972 season began with the Dolphins winning their first four games. In the fifth game of the season, Griese was tackled hard by [[Deacon Jones]] and [[Ron East]] of the [[San Diego Chargers]], and went down with a broken leg and dislocated ankle.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/16/sports/football/16morrall.html |title=An Understudy Helped Make the Dolphins 17–0 |work=The New York Times |author=Karen Crouse |date=December 16, 2007 |access-date=March 11, 2020 |archive-date=January 16, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180116190644/http://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/16/sports/football/16morrall.html |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Earl Morrall]], fresh off the waiver wire from Shula's former team, the Baltimore Colts, guided the Dolphins through the rest of the regular season, and maintained an unbeaten record in the process. Morrall also led the NFL in five passing categories during this time, including passer rating.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1972/leaders.htm |title=1972 NFL Leaders and Leaderboards |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=March 11, 2020 |archive-date=April 1, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200401001443/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1972/leaders.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> As the playoffs began, the Dolphins were not as strong as they needed to be to go deep into the postseason, barely winning against the [[Cleveland Browns]], a team that they should have beaten easily. The second game of the playoffs the team got off to a slow start against the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. Shula asked Griese to relieve the ailing Morrall, simply asking Griese at halftime, “Are you ready?” Griese replied with, “Yes, I'm ready.”{{citation needed|date=March 2020}} Griese took the field and completed 3 of 5 passes for 70 yards as the Dolphins beat the Steelers by a score of 21–17 to clinch their second straight Super Bowl appearance.

[[File:1986 Jeno's Pizza - 33 - Jim Kiick (Bob Griese crop).jpg|thumb|200px|Griese playing for the Dolphins in Super Bowl VII]]
Despite their unbeaten season, the Dolphins were listed as two point underdogs to the [[Washington Redskins]] in Super Bowl VII.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.sportingnews.com/us/other-sports/news/super-bowl-betting-history-patriots-vs-seahawks-point-spread-line-vegas-odds/qk28fzuhyadj167dsqlj2p79c |title=Super Bowl Betting History – Underdogs on Recent Roll |first=Marcus |last=DiNitto |series=The Linemakers |work=The Sporting News |date=January 25, 2015 |access-date=April 10, 2020 |archive-date=January 27, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200127182908/https://www.sportingnews.com/us/other-sports/news/super-bowl-betting-history-patriots-vs-seahawks-point-spread-line-vegas-odds/qk28fzuhyadj167dsqlj2p79c |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/page2/s/list/football/teams/greatest.html |title=Greatest NFL teams of all time |work=ESPN |quote="…the Dolphins played one of the easiest schedules in modern NFL history – the opposition had a combined winning percentage under .400." |access-date=April 10, 2020 |archive-date=August 19, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120819111835/http://espn.go.com/page2/s/list/football/teams/greatest.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Staying with the system that got them there, the Dolphins offense played a perfect ball control game. Griese completed 8 of 11 passes for 88 yards and a touchdown, and [[Larry Csonka]] rushed for over 120 yards. Washington's only score was on a returned blocked field goal,<ref>{{cite news |title=SUPER BOWL XXV; Garo's Gaffe, McGee's Hangover And More: The First 24 Years |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/01/27/sports/super-bowl-xxv-garo-s-gaffe-mcgee-s-hangover-and-more-the-first-24-years.html |newspaper=The New York Times |first=Gerald |last=Eskenazi |date=January 27, 1991 |access-date=April 10, 2020 |archive-date=October 13, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181013132859/https://www.nytimes.com/1991/01/27/sports/super-bowl-xxv-garo-s-gaffe-mcgee-s-hangover-and-more-the-first-24-years.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4oLr-bJ8Ws&t=1m50s |title=Preparation is Key with 1972 Miami Dolphins' Coach Don Shula |last=mouthpiecesports1 |date=July 31, 2008 |via=YouTube |access-date=April 10, 2020 |archive-date=March 25, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160325041716/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m4oLr-bJ8Ws&t=1m50s |url-status=live }}</ref> and Miami won the game 14–7.

In 1973, Griese led another strong Dolphins team, but they did not make it through the season undefeated. They reached the [[Super Bowl VIII|Super Bowl]] for the third consecutive season and defeated the [[Minnesota Vikings]] 24–7.

In 1974, Griese and the Dolphins had an 11–3 regular-season record, but lost to the Oakland Raiders in the divisional round of the playoffs.

In 1975, Griese and the Dolphins started strong, but late in the season in a game against the [[Baltimore Colts]], Griese suffered a broken toe and was out for the rest of the season. The Dolphins finished a respectable 10–4, but missed out on the playoffs for the first time in the Shula era.

In 1976, the Dolphins had many injuries, and the team finished the season at 6–8, the first time Don Shula ever suffered a losing season in his career.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/ShulDo0.htm |title=Don Shula Coaching Results |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |access-date=April 1, 2020 |archive-date=March 21, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321111228/https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/ShulDo0.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

===1977–1980===
The [[1977 Miami Dolphins season|1977]] season was a rebound year for both Griese and the Dolphins; he began to wear eyeglasses on the field.<ref>[https://vault.si.com/vault/1977/10/10/spectacles-make-him-spectacular Jenkins, Dan. "Spectacles make him spectacular," ''Sports Illustrated'', October 10, 1977.] Retrieved December 20, 2020</ref> On [[Thanksgiving Day (United States)|Thanksgiving]], Griese threw six touchdown passes in three quarters to defeat the [[1977 St. Louis Cardinals (NFL) season|St. Louis Cardinals]] 55–14,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=348&dat=19771125&id=3vUuAAAAIBAJ&sjid=BDMDAAAAIBAJ&pg=2809,4009275|title=Rome News-Tribune – Google News Archive Search|website=news.google.com|access-date=November 15, 2015|archive-date=November 17, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117041728/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=348&dat=19771125&id=3vUuAAAAIBAJ&sjid=BDMDAAAAIBAJ&pg=2809,4009275|url-status=live}}</ref> which set a franchise record for most points in a game;<ref>100 Things Dolphins Fans Should Know and Do Before They Die, Armando Salguero, Triumph Books, Chicago, 2020, ISBN 978-1-62937-722-3, p.176</ref> the Dolphins scored eight touchdowns and accumulated 34 first downs. He again led the AFC in touchdown passes thrown but the Dolphins rebound to a 10–4 record was again not enough to get the team into the playoffs.

The [[1978 Miami Dolphins season|following year]], Griese tore ligaments in his knee in a preseason game. However, when he came back, he was just as strong a passer as he had been the previous year. In one game against the [[1978 Houston Oilers season|Houston Oilers]] (nationally telecast as a marquee matchup on [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC's]] ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' on November 20), Griese dueled with Oiler running back [[Earl Campbell]] in an offensive slugfest. Griese threw for over 300 yards while Campbell rushed for nearly 200 and the Oilers won 35–30. For the year, Griese completed a league-leading 63% of his passes, as the Dolphins went 11–5, losing again to the Oilers in the playoffs.

[[File:1990 Bob Griese.jpg|thumb|right|Griese's bronze bust at the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]].]]
In [[1979 Miami Dolphins season|1979]], he suffered from some nagging leg injuries that affected his throwing ability. He was not as effective, and he began to hear some criticism. However, he was able to lead the Dolphins to a 10–6 record. The Dolphins then found themselves dominated by the [[1979 Pittsburgh Steelers season|Pittsburgh Steelers]] in the divisional round of the playoffs.

In [[1980 Miami Dolphins season|1980]], Griese found himself on the bench due to the emergence of [[Don Strock]] and rookie [[David Woodley]]. However, Griese came off the bench for several games in a row to lead comeback wins. Griese won back the starting spot in the fifth game of the season, but was tackled hard by [[Mike Ozdowski]] of the [[1980 Baltimore Colts season|Baltimore Colts]]. The tackle tore up his shoulder, and he was out for the rest of the year. The injury eventually led to Griese's decision to retire from the game at age 35; he was elected to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in {{nfly|1990}}.

He had established his reputation as the “Thinking Man's Quarterback,” as he brilliantly called his own plays throughout his career. Dolphins owner [[Joe Robbie]] called him “the cornerstone of the franchise,” around whom the Miami Dolphins were built. Robbie elected to ask Griese to stay on for another year as assistant coach, which he did for the 1981 season, helping Strock and the young Woodley as they teamed to become the famous “Woodstrock.” After the year ended, he decided that he did not like the hours required to be an assistant coach, hoping to devote more time to his family, yet he still enjoyed being part of the game. (Sources for Pro Football Career found in ''Undefeated'', by Bob Griese, 2000, and ''The Winning Edge'' by Don Shula, 1974.)

The Miami Dolphins had the highest winning percentage in all professional sports in the 1970s, and Griese was its starting quarterback throughout the decade, except when he was injured for several games in 1972, 1975, and 1978.

In Griese's 14 pro seasons, he threw for 25,092 yards and 192 touchdowns, and also rushed for 994 yards and seven scores. Griese was a six-time Dolphins' MVP and was All-Pro in 1971 and 1977. He played in two AFL All-Star games and six Pro Bowls.

The Dolphins retired his number 12 during a ''Monday Night Football'' game in 1985, telecast on [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], the network which would prominently be featured in his post-football career.

==Life after football==

===NBC Sports===
[[File:Nat Moore & Bob Griese at 2014 MIFF.jpg|thumb|[[Nat Moore]], guest and Griese at the 2014 [[Miami International Film Festival]]]]
To stay in touch with the game, in 1982 Griese decided to take a job as an announcer for [[NFL on NBC|NBC Sports]], teaming with [[Charlie Jones (sportscaster)|Charlie Jones]] for NFL games. While there, he called [[Super Bowl XX]].

===ABC Sports===
In 1987, Griese was hired by [[College Football on ABC|ABC Sports]], where he began to provide color commentary for college football games.<ref name=ESPN1>{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=6087452 |title=Bob Griese retires from broadcasting |date=February 3, 2011 |website=ESPN |access-date=March 11, 2020 |archive-date=April 14, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190414200158/http://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=6087452 |url-status=live }}</ref>

While at ABC, Griese called the 1999, 2001, and 2005 BCS National Championship games.

At ABC, Griese had many opportunities to watch his son [[Brian Griese]] play for the [[Michigan Wolverines]]. ABC was at first reluctant to let Griese broadcast Michigan games, fearing a conflict of interest. But when they decided to give it a try, Bob remained as impartial and professional as he could be, even referring to his son as “Griese,” rather than Brian, and pointing out errors when he felt necessary.

On January 1, 1998, Bob got to broadcast the Rose Bowl game, the last college game of his son's career. Brian was named MVP of the game, leading his Wolverines to an undefeated season and the national championship title with their Rose Bowl victory. Bob and Brian were emotional at that moment, as they thought of Bob's wife Judi, who had died from breast cancer in 1988 but whom they both felt was there at that special moment. Bob and Brian later wrote a book, entitled ''Undefeated'' ({{ISBN|0-7852-7021-3}}), which discussed not only their football connection, but also their love for Judi.

===ESPN===

During the 2009 and 2010 seasons, Griese served as the lead commentator for ESPN's noon college football broadcasts. He retired from ESPN on February 3, 2011.<ref name=ESPN1/>

===Miami Dolphins broadcasts===
Griese has been an analyst for [[List of Miami Dolphins broadcasters#Preseason television announcers|Miami Dolphins preseason TV broadcasts]] since 2002.

In 2011, he joined the [[List of Miami Dolphins broadcasters#Radio announcers|Dolphins radio broadcast team]] as a color commentator, replacing former teammate [[Jim Mandich]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/sports/fl-xpm-2011-08-19-fl-miami-dolphins-broadcast-team-0819-story.html |title=Bob Griese will replace Jim Mandich on Dolphins' broadcasts |work=South Florida Sun Sentinel |date=August 19, 2011 |access-date=March 11, 2020}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Griese married Purdue classmate Judi Lassus in June 1967,<ref name=grsmrrd>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=pxkfAAAAIBAJ&pg=5627%2C1648827 |newspaper=Tuscaloosa News |location=Alabama |agency=Associated Press |title=Griese married |date=June 11, 1967 |page=17}}</ref> following their graduation, and they had three sons: [[Brian Griese|Brian]], Jeff, and Scott. A nurse, Judi lost a six-year battle with breast cancer at age 44 in early 1988.<ref name=jdbrns>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=XEpUAAAAIBAJ&pg=5850%2C5062757 |newspaper=Boca Raton News |location=Florida |agency=Associated Press |title=Judi Griese, wife of ex-Miami Dolphin Bob Griese, dies at age 44 |date=February 15, 1988 |page=5B}}</ref><ref name=gfghv>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=_9tOAAAAIBAJ&pg=4543%2C798063|newspaper=Boca Raton News |location=Florida |agency=Associated Press |title=Griese finally gets Hall votes |date=August 3, 1990 |page=4C}}</ref> He now resides with his second wife, Shay, in [[Jupiter, Florida]] and [[Banner Elk, North Carolina]]. His youngest son is [[Brian Griese]] (b. 1975), who also played quarterback in the NFL. His grandson, Jack Griese, son of Scott, is a running back for the University of Virginia.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 22, 2022 |title=Jack Griese |url=https://virginiasports.com/player/jack-griese/ |access-date=September 2, 2023 |website=Virginia Cavaliers Official Athletic Site |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2006, Griese made an appearance on the game show, [[Wheel of Fortune (American game show)|''Wheel of Fortune'']]: he won the $100,000 grand prize and donated his $114,310 total winnings to [[Judi's House]].<ref>{{Cite episode |series=Wheel of Fortune |network=Syndication |date=January 24, 2006 |season=23 |number=4387}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=#TBT former ABC/@ESPNCFB analyst Bob Griese competed on @WheelofFortune for @JudisHouse – & son @briangriese , current ESPN #MNF analyst, was in attendance |url=https://twitter.com/ESPNFrontRow/status/1354879448349368325 |website=Twitter |access-date=February 2, 2021 |archive-date=January 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210128195041/https://twitter.com/ESPNFrontRow/status/1354879448349368325 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 1975, Griese received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement|website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#sports|access-date=November 8, 2020|archive-date=December 15, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161215023909/https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#sports|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title= 800 Feted at Glittering Banquet|date= June 29, 1975|publisher= [[American Academy of Achievement]]|url= https://achievement.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/Sunday-Courier-and-Press-June-29-1975.pdf|access-date=November 8, 2020|archive-date=May 2, 2021|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210502031818/https://achievement.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/Sunday-Courier-and-Press-June-29-1975.pdf|url-status= live}}</ref>

'''Robert Stanford Brown''' (December 8, 1941 – June 16, 2023), nicknamed "'''the Boomer'''",<ref name="Canton">{{cite web |title=Bob 'The Boomer' Brown headed to Canton |url=http://nbcsports.msnbc.com/id/5582520/ |work=NBC Sports |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=August 4, 2004 |access-date=June 4, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121009074102/http://nbcsports.msnbc.com/id/5582520/ |archive-date=October 9, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1964 through 1973. He played [[college football]] for the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska Cornhuskers]], earning [[List of unanimous All-Americans in college football|unanimous All-American]] honors. Brown was selected by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] as the [[List of second overall NFL draft picks|second overall pick]] in the [[1964 NFL draft]]. A six-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection, he played for the Eagles from 1964 to 1968, the [[Los Angeles Rams]] from 1969 to 1970, and the [[Oakland Raiders]] from 1971 to 1973. Brown was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 1993 and the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2004.

==Early life and college==
Brown was born on December 8, 1941, in [[Cleveland]], Ohio, where he later attended [[East Technical High School]].<ref name=gabriel_06182023>{{cite news|first=Kerith|last=Gabriel|title=Bob Brown, Hall of Famer and former Eagles lineman, dies at 81|date=June 18, 2023|work=The Philadelphia Inquirer|url=https://www.inquirer.com/eagles/bob-brown-dead-eagles-hall-of-fame-football-20230617.html|access-date=June 18, 2023}}</ref> He was on the football and track teams for three years.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=October 9, 1961 |title=NU's Tackle Bob Brown Says Brother Is Key to Success |work=Evening World Herald (Omaha, Nebraska0 |pages=13}}</ref> Brown was an overweight 280 pounds (127 kg) when he entered high school, and his older brother Ulysses got Brown into shape, enabling him to play football.<ref name=":0" />

Brown attended the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln|University of Nebraska]], along with Ulysses, and both were teammates on the football team.<ref name=":0" /> Brown was a [[Substitution (sport)|backup]] as an [[offensive lineman]] and [[outside linebacker]] in [[Bill Jennings (American football)|Bill Jennings]]' final season as the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Cornhuskers]]' coach in [[1961 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|1961]]. Brown became a [[starting lineup|starter]] in [[1962 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|1962]] under coach [[Bob Devaney]]. Brown preserved a 36–34 win in the [[1962 Gotham Bowl]], the program's first [[bowl game|bowl]] win, with an [[interception]] in the final minute.<ref name=mckewon_06172023/> 

As a [[senior (education)|senior]] in [[1963 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|1963]], he was a [[unanimous All-American]] selection at [[Guard (American football)|guard]], helping [[1963 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|Nebraska]] win their first conference championship since [[1940 Nebraska Cornhuskers football team|1940]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Bob Brown|publisher=National Football Foundation|url=https://footballfoundation.org/hof_search.aspx?hof=1893|access-date=June 18, 2023}}</ref> He also helped Nebraska beat [[1963 Auburn Tigers football team|Auburn]] 13–7 in the [[1964 Orange Bowl]] (played on January 1, 1964), throwing a key block that allowed teammate [[Dennis Claridge]] to run 68 yards for a touchdown.<ref>{{Cite news |date=January 2, 1964 |title=Top Draft Pick Signed by Eagles |work=The Morning Call (Allentown, Pennsylvania) |pages=49}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Orange Bowl - Nebraska vs Auburn Box Score, January 1, 1964 |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/boxscores/1964-01-01-auburn.html |access-date=2025-05-04 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> The Cornhuskers' first Black All-American,<ref name="mckewon_06172023" /> Brown was voted the Offensive Lineman of the Year by the [[Washington D.C. Touchdown Club]].<ref name="coffin2004" /> He also earned his second consecutive All-Conference selection in the [[Big Eight Conference|Big Eight]].<ref name="mckewon_06172023">{{cite web|first=Sam|last=McKewon|title=Former Nebraska OT Bob Brown, Pro and College Football Hall of Famer, dies at 81|date=June 17, 2023|work=Omaha World-Herald|url=https://omaha.com/sports/huskers/football/former-nebraska-ot-bob-brown-pro-and-college-football-hall-of-famer-dies-at-81/article_d5cca646-1e5f-569e-9475-ea4eaba0cf4e.html|access-date=June 18, 2023|archive-date=June 18, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230618020430/https://omaha.com/sports/huskers/football/former-nebraska-ot-bob-brown-pro-and-college-football-hall-of-famer-dies-at-81/article_d5cca646-1e5f-569e-9475-ea4eaba0cf4e.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Professional career==
[[File:BobBrownOAK.png|thumb|1972 Sunoco Stamp of Brown for Oakland Raiders]]
Brown was selected in the first round of the [[1964 NFL draft]] by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] with the second overall pick.<ref name="Canton"/> The contract he signed with the team had a $100,000 signing bonus.<ref name="Happy Man"/> After his rookie season in [[1964 Philadelphia Eagles season|1964]], Brown was named to the NFL All-Rookie team and earned second-team [[All-Pro]] honors.<ref>{{cite news|title=Ex-NU All-American Brown Plans To Add Weight|date=December 17, 1964|newspaper=The Lincoln Star|page=49|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-lincoln-star/126647373/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=June 18, 2023}}</ref> He was named to the [[Pro Bowl]] in [[1966 Pro Bowl|1965]] and [[1967 Pro Bowl|1966]] during his five-season career with the Eagles.<ref name="Happy Man">{{cite news |title=Bob Brown Now A Happy Man |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=jAAUAAAAIBAJ&sjid=pYoDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6039,1431616 |newspaper=The Free Lance-Star |date=May 13, 1969 |access-date=June 4, 2010 |archive-date=November 17, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117035232/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=jAAUAAAAIBAJ&sjid=pYoDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6039,1431616 |url-status=live }}</ref> After playing 50 consecutive games from his rookie year into the 1967 season, Brown suffered a knee injury, but came back and regained his form in 1968, though the Eagles were a poor 2–12 team.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |date=May 13, 1969 |title=Brown goes to Los Angeles with Nettles for Three Rams |work=The Sioux City Journal |pages=12}}</ref>

During his time with the Eagles, he had been called the top offensive lineman in the NFL, Eagles' coach [[Joe Kuharich]] calling him equal to or superior to future Hall of fame tackles [[Forrest Gregg]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Forrest Gregg, 1933-2019 {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2019/04/forrest-gregg-1933-2019/ |access-date=2025-05-04 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> and [[Jim Parker (American football)|Jim Parker]];<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jim Parker {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/jim-parker/ |access-date=2025-05-04 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> but in 1969 he demanded that Eagles general manager [[Pete Retzlaff]] trade him.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=August 30, 1966 |title=Eagles' Destructive Bob Brown Wants to Be League's Best Offensive Tackle |work=The Sioux City Journal |pages=41}}</ref> After asking for a trade from the Eagles, Brown was sent to the [[Los Angeles Rams]] in a five-player exchange on May 12, 1969. The Eagles traded Brown, along with cornerback [[Jim Nettles (American football)|Jim Nettles]], to the Rams in exchange for offensive tackle [[Joe Carollo (American football)|Joe Carollo]], guard [[Don Chuy]], and defensive back [[Irv Cross]].<ref name="Happy Man"/> Ram's future Hall of fame head coach [[George Allen (American football coach)|George Allen]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=George Allen {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/george-allen/ |access-date=2025-05-04 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> called Brown "the finest offensive lineman in pro football".<ref>{{Cite news |date=May 13, 1969 |title=LA's Allen Satisfied with Trade |work=The Sioux City Journal |pages=12}}</ref> In a [[Sport (American magazine)|''SPORT'']] magazine poll of over 1,000 players before the 1970 season, Brown was selected as the National Football Conference's top offensive lineman.<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 20, 1970 |title=Rams gain nod for Super Bowl |work=The Pocono Record |pages=15}}</ref> Brown played two All Pro and Pro Bowl seasons for the Rams in 1969-70.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Bob Brown Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BrowBo03.htm |access-date=2025-05-04 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> 

Brown was traded by the Rams to the [[Oakland Raiders]], along with two draft picks, in exchange for offensive tackle [[Harry Schuh]] and cornerback [[Kent McCloughan]] on June 23, 1971.<ref>{{cite news |title=Rams Trade Bob Brown to Oakland |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-palm-beach-post/126638825/ |newspaper=The Palm Beach Post |agency=AP|date=June 24, 1971 |page=C1|access-date=June 18, 2023|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> Raiders' future Hall of Fame coach [[John Madden]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=John Madden {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/john-madden/ |access-date=2025-05-04 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> called Brown "probably the best tackle in football".<ref>{{Cite news |date=August 28, 1971 |title=A Glance At Raiders |work=The Baltimore Sun |pages=23}}</ref> He played three seasons for the Raiders, teaming on the offensive line with fellow future Pro Football Hall of Famers [[Art Shell]], [[Gene Upshaw]], and [[Jim Otto]]. During the [[1971 Oakland Raiders season|1971 season]], another eventual Hall of Famer, [[Ron Mix]] played his final pro season as Brown's backup at right tackle.<ref>{{cite web|first=Craig|last=Ellenport|title=Unparalleled Line|date=July 24, 2004|publisher=Pro Football Hall of Fame|url=https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2004/07/news-unparalleled-line/|access-date=June 18, 2023|archive-date=May 27, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220527125629/https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2004/07/news-unparalleled-line/|url-status=live}}</ref> Hall of Fame [[Kansas City Chiefs|Kansas City Chief]] middle linebacker [[Willie Lanier]] had particular respect for Brown, among all the great offensive lineman that played for the Oakland Raiders.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |title=Behind the Bronze: Willie Lanier {{!}} Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/news/2010/10/news-behind-the-bronze-willie-lanier/ |access-date=2024-11-02 |website=pfhof |language=en}}</ref> 

He also had a reputation as the meanest lineman.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Forbes |first=Gordon |date=October 20, 1967 |title=Brown vs. Robb: It's War |work=The Philadelphia Inquirer |pages=41}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Shefski |first=Bill |date=January 25, 1967 |title=Plumb Out Of Sundays |work=Philadelphia Daily News |pages=47}}</ref> Brown said his game was predicated on inflicting more pain on the defensive lineman than would be inflicted on him. "'The guy who wins is the one who inflicts more pain. I try to drive out his intestinal fortitude. Then he's mine.'" <ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Shefski |first=Bill |date=July 25, 1968 |title=Brown: 'Ripup' Ready for New Tear |work=Philadelphia Daily News |pages=50}}</ref> When the head slap was still a legal maneuver for defensive lineman to use against offensive lineman, Brown would reverse the screws in his helmet, with the pointed ends facing out, and sharpen them.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 4, 1988 |title=Cheating in the NFL |work=The Des Moines Register |pages=41}}</ref> He was known for the exceptional force with which he delivered the "ripup" move, where an offensive lineman would drive his fists into the oncoming pass rushing defender's chest, with Brown sometimes lifting the defensive ends off their feet.<ref name=":3" />

Brown was named a first-team All-Pro during five of his ten NFL seasons. Named the NFL/NFC Offensive Lineman of the Year three times,<ref name=coffin2004>{{cite journal|title=Bob Brown|journal=The Coffin Corner|volume=26|issue=3|year=2004|url=https://profootballresearchers.org/archives/Website_Files/Coffin_Corner/26-03-1025.pdf|access-date=June 18, 2023|archive-date=May 31, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230531051406/https://www.profootballresearchers.org/archives/Website_Files/Coffin_Corner/26-03-1025.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Brown was also selected to the Pro Bowl six times: thrice with the Eagles, twice with the Rams, and once with the Raiders.<ref name="Canton"/><ref>{{cite web|title=Bob Brown|publisher=Pro Football Hall of Fame|url=https://www.profootballhof.com/players/bob-boomer-brown|access-date=June 18, 2023|archive-date=February 7, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230207080753/https://www.profootballhof.com/players/bob-boomer-brown/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":4" />

==Awards and honors==
In 1993, Brown was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Bob Brown, College Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.cfbhall.com/inductees/bob-brown-1993/ |website=cfbhall.com}}</ref> A member of the [[NFL 1960s All-Decade Team]],<ref name=mckewon_06172023/> he was inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2004.<ref name="Canton"/>  Brown's No. 64 was [[retired number|retired]] by the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] in 2004.<ref>{{cite web |author=Kaipust, Rich |title=Plans announced to celebrate Nebraska's NCAA-record sellout streak when it reaches 300 |url=http://www.theindependent.com/articles/2009/07/01/sports/huskers_hq/doc4a499c6abffa7064437025.txt |work=The Grand Island Independent |date=July 1, 2009 |access-date=June 4, 2010}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Brown was married to Cecelia and had a son, Robert Jr.<ref name=gabriel_06182023/> His son was his presenter at his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction ceremony.<ref name=gabriel_06182023/>
 
Brown had a stroke in April 2023. Afterwards, he lived in a rehabilitation center in [[Oakland, California]], where he died on June 16, 2023, at the age of 81.<ref name=gabriel_06182023/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/37870033/hall-fame-offensive-lineman-bob-brown-dies-81|publisher=[[ESPN]]|title=Hall of Fame offensive lineman Bob Brown dies at 81|date=June 17, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Bob Brown, Pro Football Hall of Fame offensive tackle, dead at 81|url=https://nypost.com/2023/06/17/bob-brown-pro-football-hall-of-famer-dead-at-81/|work=New York Post|date=June 17, 2023|access-date=June 17, 2023}}</ref>
