'''Robert Perry Golic''' (born October 26, 1957) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player, television actor, radio personality, and sports commentator.

Golic played [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 14 seasons from 1979 to 1992 with the [[New England Patriots]], [[Cleveland Browns]], and [[Los Angeles Raiders]]. He played [[college football]]  for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]], winning a national championship in 1977 and earning [[List of unanimous All-Americans in college football|unanimous All-American]] honors. In [[wrestling]], he was a two-time All-American.

He is the older brother of [[Mike Golic]] and uncle of [[Mike Golic Jr.]]

==Early life==
Golic was born in [[Cleveland|Cleveland, Ohio]] to Dorothy and [[Bob Golic (Canadian football)|Louis Robert "Bob" Golic]]. The family is of [[Slovenes|Slovenian]] descent.<ref>{{cite web |title=Slovenians on the World Stage |url=http://www.sloveniatraveltips.com/2009/01/19/slovenians-on-the-world-stage/ |access-date=March 24, 2009 |date=January 19, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090704034637/http://www.sloveniatraveltips.com/2009/01/19/slovenians-on-the-world-stage/ |archive-date=July 4, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He has two brothers, Greg and [[Mike Golic|Mike]], who also played in the NFL. His father also went by the nickname Bob; however, they are not named with the [[Suffix (name)#Generational titles|generational titles]] of junior or senior. The elder Golic had a seven year professional playing career in the [[Canadian Football League]] from 1956 to 1962.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bob Golic - CFL stats|url=http://www.justsportsstats.com/footballstatsindex.php?player_id=golicbob002}}</ref> He played for the [[Hamilton Tiger-Cats]], [[Montreal Alouettes]], and [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]]. He won the [[Grey Cup]] with Hamilton in 1957. Louis Robert Golic died on Friday, June 28, 2013, from heart failure.

Robert Perry Golic attended [[Villa Angela-St. Joseph High School|St. Joseph's High School]], at the time an all-boys school in Cleveland, where he played [[high school football]] and [[Scholastic wrestling|wrestled]]. As a high school wrestler, Golic won the Ohio high school heavyweight championship in 1975, beating Harold Smith of [[McKinley High School (Canton, Ohio)|Canton McKinley High School]], a future Olympian. He also defeated future NFL player [[Tom Cousineau]] from cross-town all-boys school rival [[St. Edward High School (Ohio)|St. Edward High School]] in [[Lakewood, Ohio]] in the tournament semifinals.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Kampf|first1=John|title=Pigskin pins: Wrestling is a football player's best offseason workout|url=http://www.news-herald.com/article/HR/20090111/NEWS/301119982|website=The News-Herald|date=April 23, 2013 |access-date=August 28, 2016}}</ref> The match between Golic and Cousineau, who placed third, has been called "one of the most memorable" in the tournament's history.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Galbincea|first1=Pat|title=Ohio's state wrestling tournament has produced more than its share of memorable moments|url=http://highschoolsports.cleveland.com/news/article/5100816392234876125/ohios-state-wrestling-tournament-has-produced-more-than-its-share-of-memorable-moments-pat-galbincea/|access-date=August 28, 2016|issue=March 3, 2010|publisher=Cleveland Plain Dealer|date=March 3, 2010}}</ref> Cousineau later was a two-time All-American at linebacker at [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State]] in [[Columbus, Ohio|Columbus]]. Golic and Cousineau eventually were teammates in the NFL with the Cleveland Browns.

==College career==
[[File:Bob Golic 1985.jpg|thumb|left|Golic in 1985]]
Golic received a [[athletic scholarship|football scholarship]] to attend the [[University of Notre Dame]] in [[Notre Dame, Indiana]], where he also wrestled. He played for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football]] team from 1975 to 1978. He was a member of the 1977 NCAA national champion football team. He was selected as a second-team All-American for the 1977 season, and a unanimous first-team All-American in 1978.

Golic was one of the nation's top collegiate wrestlers while at Notre Dame, with a three-year record of 54–4–1, finishing third in NCAA meet in 1976 and fourth in 1977.<ref name="ND1">{{cite web|title=Bob Golic Bio|url=http://www.und.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/bob_golic_134702.html|website=Notre Dame|access-date=August 28, 2016}}</ref> He was named a two-time All-American for Notre Dame as a heavyweight wrestler, capturing fourth place at the 1977 NCAA tournament and finishing third in 1978. He graduated from Notre Dame in 1979 with a B.A. degree in management. 

==Professional career==
The New England Patriots chose Golic, as a linebacker, in the second round (52nd pick overall) of the 1979 NFL Draft, and he played for the Patriots from 1979 to 1981.

Golic was cut by the Patriots going into the 1982 season and claimed on waivers by the Cleveland Browns. The Browns moved him from linebacker to nose tackle. After seven years with the Browns, he went to the Los Angeles Raiders through Plan B free agency where he played his last four NFL seasons. He was a 3-time [[Pro Bowl]]er (1985, 1986, and 1987) while playing with the Cleveland Browns.

==Post-playing career==
After retiring from football, Golic pursued an acting career. His first appearance was in ''[[Coach (TV series)|Coach]]'' on [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] playing one of Hayden Fox's former players who went on to an NFL career, but confiding to Hayden that he has cancer due to [[anabolic steroid]] use. He then appeared in ''[[Saved by the Bell: The College Years]]'', arguably his best known role, playing the role of Mike Rogers, a retired [[San Francisco 49ers]] player who became the resident adviser of Cal U, the fictional college attended by the cast. He appeared in the role for the [[NBC]] made-for-TV-movie ''[[Saved by the Bell: Wedding in Las Vegas]]'' in 1994. From 1996 until 1998, Golic also was one of the members of the original ''[[Home and Family]]'' when it aired on [[The Family Channel (American TV network, founded 2008)|The Family Channel]] (now known as [[Freeform (TV channel)|Freeform]]).

Golic hosted sports [[talk radio]] programs and did sports reporting for TV stations in [[Los Angeles]]; had a stint on [[Television in the United Kingdom|Britain's]] late 80s–90s NFL coverage on [[Channel 4]], opposite presenter [[Gary Imlach]]; served as analyst on NBC's [[NFL on NBC|NFL coverage]] from 1994 to 1996; and was a commentator for [[Spike TV|TNN]]'s coverage of the short-lived [[XFL (2001)|XFL]] in 2001. In 2004, Golic returned to [[Greater Cleveland|Northeast Ohio]] to host the afternoon [[drive time]] radio talk show on [[WNIR (FM)|WNIR]] 100.1 FM in [[Akron, Ohio]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Bob Golic – Other Works |url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0326488/otherworks |work=[[Internet Movie Database]] |access-date=April 20, 2008}}</ref> He is also a football analyst for [[WOIO]] Channel 19 in Cleveland on [[CBS]].

Golic opened a restaurant and bar in [[downtown Cleveland]]'s Warehouse District (''Bob Golic's Sports Bar & Grille'').<ref>{{cite web |title=Bob Golic part of team opening new Warehouse District pub|url=http://blog.cleveland.com/lifestyles/2008/08/bob_golic_part_of_team_opening.html |work=[[The Plain Dealer]] |date=August 12, 2008 |access-date=September 1, 2008}}</ref> The restaurant closed in June 2014. He was the vice president of Football Operations for the [[Lingerie Football League]] expansion team, the [[Cleveland Crush]] until operations ceased in 2015.<ref>{{cite web| title=Hanford Dixon named Cleveland Crush head coach| url=http://www.wkyc.com/news/article/182289/4/Hanford-Dixon-named-Cleveland-Crush-head-coach| work=www.wkyc.com| access-date=March 24, 2011| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://archive.today/20130105065815/http://www.wkyc.com/news/article/182289/4/Hanford-Dixon-named-Cleveland-Crush-head-coach| archive-date=January 5, 2013| df=mdy-all}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Golic is the older brother of [[Mike Golic]], who is a former NFL football player and was a radio host, first as half of [[ESPN Radio]]'s ''[[Mike & Mike]]'', followed by ESPN Radio's ''[[Golic and Wingo]]''. His nephews are [[Mike Golic Jr.]], himself a former football player turned radio host,<ref>[http://www.und.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/golicjr_mike00.html Mike Golic Jr Profile] University of Notre Dame. Retrieved March 22, 2009</ref> and Jake, who began studying at the University of Notre Dame in 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://sports.rightpundits.com/?p=602 |title=Jake Golic is Notre Dame's First Signee |access-date=March 23, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080613021625/http://sports.rightpundits.com/?p=602 |archive-date=June 13, 2008 |url-status=dead  }}</ref>

Mike Golic is a spokesperson for [[Nutrisystem]] after losing more than {{cvt|50|lb}} on the diet; however, Bob Golic has outdone his younger brother, dropping more than {{cvt|140|lb}}, returning to his high school weight of {{cvt|245|lb}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ex-Browns lineman Bob Golic tackles a diet and loses 140 pounds in 8 months|url=http://www.cleveland.com/living/plaindealer/index.ssf?/base/living-1/1210926696191250.xml&coll=2|work=[[The Plain Dealer]]|access-date=May 16, 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607140121/http://www.cleveland.com/living/plaindealer/index.ssf?%2Fbase%2Fliving-1%2F1210926696191250.xml&coll=2|archive-date=June 7, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> Bob Golic married Jacquelyn Benlein in 1983 and they had a child before divorcing in 1992.

Golic lives with his family in [[Solon, Ohio]]. He and Karen Baughman married in 1996 and they have two children. Karen was a [[Ballet dancer|ballerina]] and [[Oakland Raiderettes|Raiderette]] with the [[Oakland Raiders]]. Bob performed ''[[The Nutcracker]]'' with Karen at the [[Akron Civic Theatre]] in Akron in 2006.<ref>{{cite news |title=Seasonal 'Nutcracker' at Akron Civic |url=http://www.stowsentry.com/news/article/1393771 |work=Stow Sentry |publisher=Record Publishing |location=Stow, Ohio |date=November 22, 2006 |access-date=March 25, 2009 |quote=CBT welcomes to the stage, for the Nov. 25, 7p.m. performance, former Cleveland Browns player Bob Golic and his wife Karen. The two will dance in the party scene together. |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716152613/http://www.stowsentry.com/news/article/1393771 |archive-date=July 16, 2011  }}</ref>

'''Robert Glenn Baumhower''' (born August 4, 1955) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] for the [[Miami Dolphins]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Alabama Crimson Tide]] under coach [[Bear Bryant]] from 1973 to 1976 and professionally for Miami under coach [[Don Shula]]. He later became a restaurateur.

==Early life and college==
Baumhower attended Palm Beach Gardens High School in Florida for two seasons before playing at Tuscaloosa High School his senior year.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uxYYRXEv6U0C&q=%22bob+baumhower%22+%22tuscaloosa+high+school%22&pg=PA98|title=Game of My Life Alabama Crimson Tide: Memorable Stories of Crimson Tide Football|first=Tommy|last=Hicks|date=2011|publisher=Skyhorse Publishing Inc.|isbn=9781613210079|access-date=June 24, 2017|via=Google Books}}</ref>

Playing as a defensive tackle in college at the [[University of Alabama]] under coach [[Bear Bryant]], Baumhower helped lead the [[Alabama Crimson Tide football|Crimson Tide]] to two 11–1 records as well as a 31–4 overall record. He was part of the [[1974 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|1974 team]] which lost to [[1974 Notre Dame Fighting Irish football team|Notre Dame]] in the [[1975 Orange Bowl|Orange Bowl]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/alabama/1974-roster.html|title=1974 Alabama Crimson Tide Roster|website=Sports-Reference.com|access-date=May 17, 2017}}</ref> the [[1975 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|1975 team]] which defeated [[1975 Penn State Nittany Lions football team|Penn State]] in the [[1975 Sugar Bowl|Sugar Bowl]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/alabama/1975-roster.html|title=1975 Alabama Crimson Tide Roster|website=Sports-Reference.com|access-date=May 17, 2017}}</ref> and the [[1976 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|1976 team]] which won the [[1976 Liberty Bowl|Liberty Bowl]] over [[1976 UCLA Bruins football team|UCLA]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/alabama/1976-roster.html|title=1976 Alabama Crimson Tide Roster|website=Sports-Reference.com|access-date=May 17, 2017}}</ref> Baumhower was a first-team [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-Southeastern Conference]] selection in both 1975 and 1976.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1891&dat=19751201&id=bHsjAAAAIBAJ&pg=2406,53834&hl=en|work=Gadsden Times|date=December 1, 1975|access-date=August 12, 2017|author=Ed Shearer|title=Cook, DuBose head All-SEC Selection}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1798&dat=19761123&id=BoY1AAAAIBAJ&pg=5374,4682657&hl=en|title=Cowans Sole Gator on All-SEC Team|work=Sarasota Journal|date=November 23, 1976}}</ref> After the 1976 season, he was invited to play in the [[Senior Bowl]] college all-star game.<ref>{{cite news|title=Top College Passer To Lead South|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/13044166/top_college_passer_to_lead_south/|access-date=August 12, 2017|work=York Daily Record|agency=United Press International|date=December 9, 1976|page=24|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

==Professional career==
Baumhower was drafted by the Dolphins with the 40th overall pick (second round) in the 1977 [[NFL Draft|NFL draft]], behind the first round pick, another defensive lineman from the [[Southeastern Conference]], [[A. J. Duhe]] of [[Louisiana State University|LSU]]; earning a spot on the 1977 All-Rookie team. Baumhower and Duhe would share the 1977 Defensive Rookie of the Year honors.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/awards/nfl-all-rookie-1977.htm|title=1977 NFL All-Rookie Team|website=pro-football-reference.com|access-date=September 22, 2017}}</ref> He was selected five times to the [[Pro Bowl]] in the NFL.

Baumhower and Duhe, who eventually was moved to inside linebacker, formed the heart of the Dolphins' "Killer B's"<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.miamidolphins.com/news/article-1/Rummaging-Through-The-Attic-A-Bee-utiful-Poster/2b2b7b8a-3b7a-4769-b319-e6927f9c5c3c|title=Rummaging Through The Attic: A Bee-utiful Poster|website=miamidolphins.com|access-date=June 24, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170701150713/http://www.miamidolphins.com/news/article-1/Rummaging-Through-The-Attic-A-Bee-utiful-Poster/2b2b7b8a-3b7a-4769-b319-e6927f9c5c3c|archive-date=July 1, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> defense of the late 1970s through mid-1980s, coached by defensive coordinator [[Bill Arnsparger]]. Baumhower was flanked on the line by ends [[Doug Betters]] and [[Kim Bokamper]], while other stars of the unit included outside linebacker [[Bob Brudzinski]] and defensive backs [[Lyle Blackwood]] and [[Glenn Blackwood]]. The unit was ranked first in the NFL in total defense in 1982, when Miami reached [[Super Bowl XVII]].

The 1983 season may have been Baumhower's best as he was named NFL Defensive Player of the Year (Pro Football Weekly), first-team All-Pro (Associated Press),  first-team All-AFC (United Press International) and a starter in the Pro Bowl game. He was a first-team All-NFL selection in 1981 and 1983 and first-team All-AFC in 1979, 1981 and 1983.

Baumhower would retire after the 1986 season. He was inducted into the Alabama Sports Hall of Fame in 1995.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ashof.org/index.php?src=directory&view=company&srctype=detail&refno=258&category=Football|title=Alabama Sports Hall of Fame - Bob Baumhower|website=ashof.org|access-date=September 22, 2017}}</ref>

On December 14, 2008, Baumhower was inducted into [[The Miami Dolphin Honor Roll]] during a ceremony at [[Dolphin Stadium]] (now [[Hard Rock Stadium]]).

'''Robert Frank Gagliano''' (born September 5, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and the [[United States Football League]] (USFL). Gagliano began his career playing for [[Herbert Hoover High School (Glendale)|Hoover High School]] in [[Glendale, California]], then continued playing for [[Glendale Community College (California)|Glendale Community College]]. He then played for [[United States International University]] in [[San Diego, California|San Diego]] before transferring to [[Utah State University]].
==Professional Football==
Gagliano was selected by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] in the 12th round of the [[1981 NFL draft]]. Gagliano appeared in two games over three seasons for the Chiefs, attempting and completing just one pass for seven yards. After being released by Kansas City in 1984, Gagliano signed with the USFL's [[Denver Gold]]. In 1985, he took over as the full-time starting quarterback and had his most productive season as a professional, throwing for 2,695 yards and 13 touchdowns with 17 interceptions while leading the Gold to the playoffs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/g/gagl00200.html|title=Bob Gagliano Pro Football Stats|website=ProFootballArchives.com}}</ref> Following the USFL's collapse, Gagliano was signed by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in 1986 but did not see action during his first season. In 1987, he was released by the team before the regular season, but was re-signed as a replacement player after the [[National Football League Players Association|NFLPA]] went on strike. In his only career start for the 49ers, Gagliano led them to a 41-21 victory over the replacement [[New York Giants]] on [[Monday Night Football]]. The next week, he relinquished the starting quarterback position to veteran [[Joe Montana]], who led other regular players who crossed the picket line. Gagliano relieved Montana during the game and threw for 79 yards and a TD in the 49ers' 25-17 win.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GaglBo00/gamelog/|title=Bob Gagliano Career Game Log|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref> After spending 1988 on the rosters of three different teams (Tampa Bay, Houston, Indianapolis), he was signed by the [[Detroit Lions]] in 1989. He appeared in 11 games, starting seven and led the Lions to five consecutive victories to close out the season. The following season, he  started four out of the name games he played in. It was during his two years in Detroit that he was first pegged with the nickname "'''the Goose'''".<ref>{{cite web|title=GAGLIANO, BOB 'GOOSE'|date=February 21, 2015 |url=http://lee.n8d.com/2015/gagliano-bob-goose/}}</ref> Gagliano spent 1991 and 1992 with the [[San Diego Chargers]], playing in seven games with one start. In 1994, rookie [[Perry Klein]] beat him out for the No. 3 quarterback slot with the [[Atlanta Falcons]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/08/23/sports/football-klein-cw-post-quarterback-is-sticking-with-falcons.html|title=FOOTBALL; Klein, C.W. Post Quarterback, is Sticking with Falcons|newspaper=The New York Times|date=23 August 1994}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Following his pro football career, Gagliano became an insurance executive but continued his involvement in the sport by conducting youth football camps. In 1999, Gagliano was hired as a technical consultant for ''[[The Replacements (film)|The Replacements]]'', a 2000 film that depicted a fictional pro football team. Gagliano served as a personal tutor for actor [[Keanu Reeves]], teaching him how to believably play the quarterback position.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.sfgate.com/sports/article/A-one-day-starter-in-49ers-heyday-2500048.php|title=A one-day starter in 49ers' heyday|website=SFGate.com|date=30 September 2007}}</ref>

'''Robert Lee Grim''' (born May 8, 1945) is an American former professional [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played in the league from 1967 to 1977.

==High school and college career==
He played [[high school football]] at Red Bluff High School and [[college football]] at [[Oregon State University]].  In 1964, as a sophomore, he started at left end for the Beavers, helping to lead the team to the 1965 Rose Bowl.  The 1965 Rose Bowl remains Oregon State's last Rose Bowl appearance.

==Professional career==
After the 1966–1967 NFL football season, the [[Minnesota Vikings]] traded Fran Tarkenton for four draft picks in the [[1967 NFL draft]].  The Vikings used one of the four, a second round draft pick, to acquire Grim.  He played with them for five seasons, helping them to the 1969 NFL championship and a [[Super Bowl IV]] appearance. He was traded along with [[Norm Snead]], [[Vince Clements]], a first rounder in [[1972 NFL draft|1972]] (24th overall–[[Larry Jacobson]]) and a second rounder in [[1973 NFL draft|1973]] (40th overall–[[Brad Van Pelt]]) from the Vikings to the Giants for [[Fran Tarkenton]] on January 27, 1972.<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1972/01/28/archives/vikings-get-tarkenton-for-snead-and-4-others.html Koppett, Leonard. "Vikings Get Tarkenton For Snead and 4 Others," ''The New York Times'', Friday, January 28, 1972.] Retrieved November 1, 2020</ref><ref>[https://www.prosportstransactions.com/football/DraftTrades/Years/1972.htm 1972 NFL Draft Pick Transactions, February 1 (Rounds 1–7) & 2 (Rounds 8–17) – Pro Sports Transactions.] Retrieved November 1, 2020</ref> He played with the Giants for three seasons and the [[Chicago Bears]] for a season.  Grim ended his career, playing with Fran Tarkenton and the Vikings for his final two seasons, helping the team to the 1976 NFC championship and a [[Super Bowl XI]] appearance.  Grim ended his career having played in 133 total games.

'''Robert Hayden Avellini''' (August 28, 1953 – May 4, 2024) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily with the [[Chicago Bears]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Maryland Terrapins football|Maryland Terrapins]] and was selected by the Bears in the sixth round of the [[1975 NFL draft]]. He finished his career with the [[New York Jets]], for whom he did not appear in a game.

==Professional career==
Avellini played [[college football]] at the [[University of Maryland]] and was a sixth round selection of the Bears in the [[1975 NFL draft]]. As a rookie with Chicago in [[1975 Chicago Bears season|1975]], he started four games on a team that finished 4–10, throwing for 942 yards with 6 touchdown passes along with 11 interceptions.

He played for the Bears from 1975 to 1984, primarily serving as a backup quarterback during his NFL career. Fully established as the Bears starter in [[1976 Chicago Bears season|1976]], Avellini started all 14 games, throwing for 1,580 yards, although with 15 interceptions to only 8 touchdowns. Chicago improved to a 7–7 mark. Avellini improved those numbers in [[1977 Chicago Bears season|1977]], passing for 2,004 yards while once again starting every game for the Bears. His interception rate was rather high, throwing 18 picks compared to only 11 touchdown passes. The Bears showed improvement as they tied the [[1977 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]] for the [[NFC Central]] title at 9–5 and earned a trip to the playoffs as the wildcard team, where they were handily beaten by the [[1977 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]]. [[Walter Payton]]'s season of over 1,800 yards rushing had much to do with their success.

In [[1978 Chicago Bears season|1978]], the Bears struggled.  They started 4–8 with Avellini under center, as he threw for 16 interceptions, while tossing only 5 touchdown passes. This caused coach [[Neill Armstrong]] to make a switch at quarterback, inserting  veteran [[Mike Phipps]] into the starting role.<ref>[http://www.bearshistory.com/seasons/1979chicagobears.aspx 1979 Chicago Bears<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> Phipps, for whom the Bears had traded their first-round pick in the 1978 draft to acquire from the Cleveland Browns, won 3 out of the final 4 games, to establish himself as the starter for the next season.  The Bears surprisingly rolled to a 10–6 record in [[1979 Chicago Bears season|1979]], tying the record of the division champion Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and Avellini was now the backup. He continued in this capacity, playing behind Phipps, [[Vince Evans]], and [[Jim McMahon]] until the [[1984 Chicago Bears season|1984]] season, seeing little action on the field.

In 1984, with the Bears starting 2–0, Jim McMahon was injured and [[Mike Ditka]] inserted Avellini as the starter for a road game against the Green Bay Packers.<ref>[http://www.bearshistory.com/seasons/1984chicagobears.aspx 1984 Chicago Bears<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> Avellini had started only five games since the end of the 1978 season. The Bears mustered little offense with Avellini at the controls, but still managed to edge the [[1984 Green Bay Packers season|Packers]] 9–7. Chicago struggled the next week as they were soundly beaten by the [[1984 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] 38–9. This resulted in Avellini being cut from the Bears' roster by Ditka, ending his decade-long tenure with Chicago. Avellini signed with the [[1984 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] in mid-November, where he ended his playing career after the 1984 season. The Jets released him before the 1985 season.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1985/09/02/The-New-York-Jets-waived-five-players-Monday-including/1294494481600/|title=The New York Jets waived five players Monday, including veteran quarterback Bob Avellini, to reach the mandatory NFL regular-season limit of 45|access-date=September 10, 2021}}</ref> The Bears, meanwhile, went to the NFC Championship game in 1984 and won [[Super Bowl XX]] in [[1985 NFL season|1985]]. Avellini made a brief comeback in [[1986 Dallas Cowboys season|1986]] with the Dallas Cowboys, starting three preseason games, but was released at the final cut deadline.

==Legal troubles==
In May 2009, Avellini was arrested for [[driving under the influence]] and acquitted for the third time. He had been convicted of the offense in 2002. In October 2013, a DuPage County grand jury indicted Avellini on felony drunken driving charges a week after his sixth DUI-related arrest since 2002.  On November 19, 2014, Avellini was sentenced to 18 months in prison for his 3rd DUI.<ref>[https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=4147705 Avellini acquitted of DUI again], ESPN, May 6, 2009.</ref> Avellini declared bankruptcy on February 27, 2012, listing debts of more than $2.2 million and assets of $1.3 million.

==Personal life and death==
Avellini was actively involved in a number of Chicago area charitable organizations. Along with a real estate career, he appeared on several Chicago radio and television sports shows.{{citation needed|date=January 2015}}

Avellini died from pancreatic<ref>[https://www.haysfuneralhome.com/obituaries/Robert-H-Avellini?obId=31394349]</ref> cancer on May 4, 2024, at the age of 70.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bob Avellini, Bears QB who teamed with Walter Payton, dies |url=https://www.espn.co.uk/nfl/story/_/id/40085401/bob-avellini-bears-qb-teamed-walter-payton-dies |access-date=5 May 2024 |publisher=ESPN |date=5 May 2024}}</ref><ref>[https://www.chicagobears.com/news/former-bears-qb-bob-avellini-passes-away Former Bears QB Bob Avellini passes away]</ref>

'''Robert Chadwick Berry Jr.''' (March 10, 1942 – April 17, 2023) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for twelve seasons. He was selected to one [[Pro Bowl]] in [[1970 Pro Bowl|1969]] as a member of the [[1969 Atlanta Falcons season|Atlanta Falcons]]. Berry was a member of three [[Super Bowl]] teams with the [[Minnesota Vikings]] in the mid-1970s.

==College career==
Born and raised in [[San Jose, California]], Berry played [[High school football|football]] at [[Willow Glen High School]], where his father was a longtime head coach.<ref name=cococo>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2245&dat=19621220&id=Y7QzAAAAIBAJ&sjid=hzIHAAAAIBAJ&pg=3563,6711579 |newspaper=Lodi News-Sentinel |location=California |title=Berry-Troppmann co-coaches |date=December 20, 1962 |page=10 }}</ref><ref name=bpconfsd>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=RMkRAAAAIBAJ&sjid=JOkDAAAAIBAJ&pg=1663%2C94964 |newspaper=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington |agency=Associated Press |title=Berry's parents confused |date=November 1, 1963 |page=14 }}</ref><ref name=dsprb>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=RjlWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=regDAAAAIBAJ&pg=3174%2C2872398 |work=Spokesman-Review |location=Spokane, Washington |agency=(University of Oregon Athletics)|last=Childs |first=Hall |title=Duck staff praises Berry |date=October 9, 1964 |page=14}}</ref> He graduated in 1960 and played [[college football]] at [[Oregon Ducks football|Oregon]],<ref name=cbbfhwb>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Wv1VAAAAIBAJ&sjid=8uIDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6802%2C1009093 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |last=Leutzinger |first=Jerry |title=Cocky Bob Berry figures he's Webfoots' best quarterback |date=September 6, 1962 |page=3D}}</ref> where he was a three-year letter winner under head coach [[Len Casanova]].<ref name=dsprb/> At Oregon, Berry teamed with future [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]]rs [[Mel Renfro]] and [[Dave Wilcox]] and led the Ducks to three consecutive winning seasons. In his junior year in [[1963 Oregon Ducks football team|1963]], Oregon's last as an [[NCAA Division I FBS independent schools|independent]], the Ducks beat [[1963 SMU Mustangs football team|SMU]] 21–14 in the [[1963 Sun Bowl|Sun Bowl]] on New Year's Eve.<ref name=blott>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=8eoxAAAAIBAJ&sjid=EuMDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5745%2C75008 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |last=Uhrhammer |first=Jerry |title=Berry leads Oregon to 21–14 win |date=January 1, 1963 |page=1D }}</ref> (The [[Pac-12 Conference|Pacific-8]] conference did not allow a second bowl team until [[1975 NCAA Division I football season|1975]]).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eugene Register-Guard – Google News Archive Search |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Ua5VAAAAIBAJ&sjid=POADAAAAIBAJ&pg=5990,1304396 |access-date=April 24, 2023 |website=news.google.com}}</ref>

Berry was named a first-team [[1964 All-America college football team|All-American]] after his senior season, despite being edged out as All-Pacific-8 quarterback by [[Craig Morton]] of [[1964 California Golden Bears football team|California]]. In the [[1964 NCAA University Division football season#Heisman Trophy|balloting]] for the [[Heisman Trophy]] won by [[John Huarte]] of [[1964 Notre Dame Fighting Irish football team|Notre Dame]], Berry was thirteenth, just behind [[Joe Namath]] ([[1964 Alabama Crimson Tide football team|Alabama]]) and [[Gale Sayers]] ([[1964 Kansas Jayhawks football team|Kansas]]).<ref name=hwnhsmn>{{cite news |url=http://archives.chicagotribune.com/1964/11/25/page/35/article/huarte-wins-heisman-gridiron-trophy |newspaper=Chicago Tribune|agency=Associated Press |title=Huarte wins Heisman gridiron trophy |date=November 25, 1964 |page=1, sec. 3 }}</ref><ref name=jhhsmn64>{{cite web |url=http://heisman.com/roster.aspx?rp_id=30&path=football |work=Heisman Trophy |title=John Huarte |date=1964 |access-date=January 25, 2017}}</ref> His teammates named him the outstanding player and he played in the [[East–West Shrine Bowl|East-West Shrine Game]] and the [[Hula Bowl]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bob Berry – Football {{!}} Oregon Sports Hall of Fame & Museum |url=https://oregonsportshall.org/timeline/bob-berry-football/ |access-date=April 24, 2023 |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 1985, Berry received the university's distinguished alumnus award. Berry was inducted to the Oregon Sports Hall of Fame in 1987 and the University of Oregon Sports Hall of Fame in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hall of Fame Candidate Capsule: Bob Berry |url=https://footballfoundation.org/news/2012/3/13/_51415.aspx |access-date=April 24, 2023 |website=National Football Foundation |language=en}}</ref>

==Professional career==
===Minnesota Vikings (first stint)===
Selected by the [[1964 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] in the eleventh round of the [[1964 NFL draft]]<ref name=fwbfdbn>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=FpwRAAAAIBAJ&sjid=a-MDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6811%2C590201 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |title=Four Webfoots drafted by NFL |date=December 3, 1963 |page=2B}}</ref> and by the [[1964 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]] in the twenty-sixth round of the [[1964 American Football League draft|1964 AFL draft]], Berry played his senior season at Oregon in 1964 and signed with the [[Minnesota Vikings]] in late November.<ref name=vbvbry>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=T_1VAAAAIBAJ&sjid=9-IDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5174%2C4749993 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |last=Strite |first=Dick |title=Van Brocklin visits Berry |date=November 24, 1964 |page=2B }}</ref><ref name=bspc>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=VP1VAAAAIBAJ&sjid=9-IDAAAAIBAJ&pg=1335%2C5577203 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |agency=Associated Press |title=Berry signs pro contract |date=November 29, 1964 |page=1B }}</ref> Minnesota had acquired his draft rights in an off-season trade with the Eagles.<ref name=vsbb >{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=OjxYAAAAIBAJ&sjid=aPcDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5450%2C5099667 |newspaper=The Bulletin |location=Bend, Oregon |agency=UPI |title=Vikings sign Bob Berry |date=November 30, 1964 |page=8 }}</ref> Berry was out of college during the 1961 season, a de facto [[Redshirt (college sports)|redshirt]] year.<ref name=cbbfhwb/><ref name=btskip>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=e88zAAAAIBAJ&sjid=7fcDAAAAIBAJ&pg=1225%2C6523483 |newspaper=The Bulletin |location=Bend, Oregon |agency=UPI |title=Berry to skip '61 grid play |date=July 11, 1961 |page=2}}</ref>

[[File:Berry-Bob-game-1971.jpg|thumb|left|280px|Berry in action against the Detroit Lions, October 1971.]]
Berry played three seasons with the Vikings, the first two under head coach [[Norm Van Brocklin]], himself a former Oregon quarterback, and was primarily a reserve behind [[Fran Tarkenton]]. He made his first start in [[1966 Minnesota Vikings season|1966]], a loss in the snow at home to the expansion [[1966 Atlanta Falcons season|Atlanta Falcons]] on December 4.<ref name=icsnhabe>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=RfFVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=_eADAAAAIBAJ&pg=3928%2C1228039 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |agency=Associated Press |title=Ice, snow hamper Berry |date=December 5, 1966 |page=4B}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Boxscore finder: all games started at QB by Bob Berry in 1966 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/game_query.cgi?qb=BerrBo00&yr=1966 |website=pro-football-reference.com |access-date=June 11, 2010}}</ref> Following the 1966 season, Tarkenton demanded to be traded and was sent to the [[1967 New York Giants season|New York Giants]] for multiple draft picks and Van Brocklin stepped down as head coach.<ref name=gtdchftk>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=wJocAAAAIBAJ&sjid=ymUEAAAAIBAJ&pg=7232%2C1897567 |newspaper=Sarasota Herald-Tribune |location=Florida |agency=Associated Press |title=Giants trade draft picks for Tarkenton |date=March 8, 1967 |page=18 }}</ref> [[Joe Kapp]] was the starting quarterback under new head coach [[Bud Grant]] in [[1967 New York Giants season|1967]] and Berry saw very limited action.<ref name=cmbokp>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=uNpNAAAAIBAJ&sjid=24oDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6834%2C4029583 |newspaper=Free Lance-Star |agency=Associated Press |last=Hallman |first=Charles |title=Cuozzo may beat out Kapp |date=August 10, 1968 |page=6 }}</ref> In training camp in [[1968 Minnesota Vikings season|1968]], Berry was behind Kapp and [[Gary Cuozzo]] (acquired in a trade with the [[New Orleans Saints]]) and missed the final cut in early September.<ref name=btcbmv>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Fq1VAAAAIBAJ&sjid=BOEDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5683%2C2120893 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |title=Berry, Tobey cut by Minnesota Viks |date=September 10, 1968 |page=3B }}</ref>

===Atlanta Falcons===
Berry was quickly picked up by the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in [[1968 Atlanta Falcons season|1968]],<ref name=fpuflb>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=xyseAAAAIBAJ&sjid=O5sEAAAAIBAJ&pg=2074%2C2212502 |newspaper=Tuscaloosa News |title=Falcons pick up Flatley, Berry |agency=Associated Press |date=September 11, 1968 |page=16 }}</ref> and Van Brocklin became the head coach after the third game of the season.<ref name=rsprvb>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=U9hVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=H-EDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5185%2C311260 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |agency=Associated Press |last=Speer |first=Ron |title=Van to have 5-year pact |date=October 2, 1968 |page=1D }}</ref> Berry started 51 games for the Falcons in five seasons, through [[1972 Atlanta Falcons season|1972]], throwing for 8,489 yards and 57 touchdowns, with a [[passer rating]] of 79.2.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bob Berry |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BerrBo00.htm |website=pro-football-reference.com |access-date=June 11, 2010}}</ref> He was selected to the [[Pro Bowl]] in [[1970 Pro Bowl|1969]]. In May 1973, he was traded back to the Vikings for QB [[Bob Lee (quarterback)|Bob Lee]].<ref name=bttvks>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=keVVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=E-EDAAAAIBAJ&pg=2013%2C3310482 |work=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=Associated Press |title=Berry traded to Viks for Warwick, Lee |date=May 14, 1973 |page=3B}}</ref><ref name=bbwiort>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=QwQqAAAAIBAJ&sjid=zigEAAAAIBAJ&pg=7400%2C4305927 |newspaper=Milwaukee Journal |agency=press dispatches |title=Berry back with Vikings and old rival, Tarkenton |date=May 15, 1973 |page=15, part 2 |access-date=November 15, 2015 |archive-date=May 6, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160506003532/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=QwQqAAAAIBAJ&sjid=zigEAAAAIBAJ&pg=7400,4305927 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Minnesota Vikings (second stint)===
Berry played for the Minnesota Vikings again for four seasons, beginning in [[1973 Minnesota Vikings season|1973]]. He was again the backup to Tarkenton, and Minnesota played in three Super Bowls ([[Super Bowl VIII|VIII]], [[Super Bowl IX|IX]], and [[Super Bowl XI|XI]]) during this second stint, all losses. Berry retired from football on the first day of [[1977 Minnesota Vikings season|1977]] training camp, July 28; Berry's position with the Vikings became tenuous when they drafted [[Tommy Kramer]] from [[Rice Owls football|Rice]] three months earlier.<ref name=pbbret>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=lv4iAAAAIBAJ&sjid=U80FAAAAIBAJ&pg=849,6781194 |newspaper=Palm Beach Post |agency=wire services |title=Tarkenton's backup Berry retires |date=July 29, 1977 |page=D2 |access-date=November 15, 2015 |archive-date=November 17, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117040150/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=lv4iAAAAIBAJ&sjid=U80FAAAAIBAJ&pg=849,6781194 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Berry had a daughter, Jennifer (born 1972) and a son, Michael (born 1993) and two grandchildren. Berry resided in [[Santa Cruz, California]].<ref>{{cite web| title=RetroDuck – Bob Berry | website=DuckSportsAuthority | date=July 22, 2002 | url=https://oregon.rivals.com/news/retroduck-bob-berry | access-date=April 20, 2023}}</ref>

Berry's younger brother Ken was the starting quarterback at [[San Jose State Spartans football|San Jose State]], and their two teams met in 1963.<ref name=bpconfsd/><ref name=babab>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=pp0RAAAAIBAJ&sjid=UuMDAAAAIBAJ&pg=4709%2C27825 |newspaper=Eugene Register Guard |title=Berrys hoping to see Berry against Berry |date=November 1, 1963 |page=3B }}</ref><ref name=hdfts>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=QvxVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=UuMDAAAAIBAJ&pg=5527%2C244994 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |title=Helpless Ducks fall, 13–7 |date=November 3, 1963 |page=1B }}</ref>

Berry died in Santa Cruz on April 17, 2023, at the age of 81.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Charean |date=April 21, 2023 |title=Former Vikings, Falcons quarterback Bob Berry dies at 81 |url=https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2023/04/20/former-vikings-falcons-quarterback-bob-berry-dies-at-81/ |access-date=April 24, 2023 |website=ProFootballTalk |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''Robert Paul Breunig''' (born July 4, 1953) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for the [[Dallas Cowboys]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Arizona State Sun Devils]]. A three-time [[Pro Bowl]] section, he won a [[Super Bowl]] with the Cowboys.

==Early life==
Breunig attended [[Alhambra High School (Phoenix, Arizona)|Alhambra High School]] in [[Phoenix, Arizona]], where he played on the 1967 freshman football A Team that was 10-0 and he was named most valuable player. He also received a varsity letter on the wrestling team as a freshman.

Bob played on the varsity football team in 1968 as a sophomore and was a leading tackler in a number of games. 
in his junior year, in 1969, he was named Second-team All State and the Team Most Valuable Defensive Player. 
In 1970 as a senior, the team went 8–2, still the best record in Alhambra HS history, Bob led the team in scoring, rushing and tackling as a [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] and [[middle linebacker]], receiving All-State "Defensive Captain" honors. He was named the team MVP.

He was also the [[wrestling]] 1971 AAA Heavyweight State Champion achieving a 42–1 record during his junior and senior seasons.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://archive.azcentral.com/sports/preps/articles/20100806bob-breunig-arizona-high-school-hall-of-fame.html | title=Wrestling matches taught Bob Breunig well | accessdate=March 5, 2016}}</ref>

In 2000, he was included in the ''[[Arizona Republic]]''{{'s}} "Athletes of the Century" list and to the Arizona All-Century high school football team. In 2010, he was inducted into the Arizona High School Sports Hall of Fame.

==College career==
Breunig signed with [[Arizona State University]] out of Phoenix Alhambra High School and became a starter by his second year (NCAA football freshmen were then ineligible), leading the team in tackles with 91 (incl. 19 against the [[Air Force Academy]]). He would remain the team leader in tackles with 117 as a junior and 145 as a senior. He was a First-team All American ([[Kodak]], ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'', ''[[Sporting News]]'', [[Pop Warner]]), a Second-team All American (AP and UPI), a two-time [[Western Athletic Conference|WAC]] Defensive Player of the Year and a three-time All-[[Western Athletic Conference|WAC]] selection. He played in the [[East-West Shrine Game]], the [[Hula Bowl]] and the [[Coaches All-America Game]].<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.azcentral.com/story/sports/college/asu/2015/01/09/former-asu-lb-bob-breunig-selected-to-the-college-hof/21499179/ | title=Former ASU LB Bob Breunig selected to the College Hall of Fame | accessdate=March 5, 2016}}</ref>

He was a part of two 10-win seasons, a 28–8 overall record, two [[Fiesta Bowl]] wins, and the 1972 and 1973 [[Western Athletic Conference]] championships. He starred for three nationally ranked teams from 1972 to 1974. In 1999, he was chosen as the Butkus Silver Anniversary Award Winner, and in 1996, he was named to the ASU "All Time Team" [[Arizona State University]] and [[Western Athletic Conference]] 20 Year Team.

He graduated holding the career total tackles record (353), the career solo tackles record (206) and the single-season records for both categories. He was named team MVP as a senior, was a Team Captain twice.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://footballfoundation.org/news/2012/3/14/_51418.aspx?path=football| title=Hall of Fame Candidate Capsule: Bob Breunig | date=March 14, 2012 | access-date=March 5, 2016}}</ref>

As a freshman at ASU, Breunig wrestled on the varsity team for one year, finishing with a 10–4 record. He was selected as the Phoenix Press Box Association Amateur Athlete of the Year in 1974. He graduated with a Bachelor of Science degree in Business Marketing in 1977.

In 1977, he was inducted into [[Arizona State University]] Athletic Hall of Fame. In 2012, he was inducted into the Sun Devil Football Ring of Honor. In 2015, he was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]].

==Professional career==
Breunig was selected in the third round (70th overall) of the [[1975 NFL draft]], as part of the Dallas Cowboys' [[Dirty Dozen (American football)|Dirty Dozen draft]]. In [[1976 NFL season|1976]], he became a starter at [[strongside linebacker]], replacing the retired [[Dave Edwards (linebacker)|Dave Edwards]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1955&dat=19760912&id=J8otAAAAIBAJ&sjid=BqEFAAAAIBAJ&pg=5086,1088616&hl=es | title=Dallas Choice Over Eagles | accessdate=March 5, 2016}}</ref>

In [[1977 NFL season|1977]], he replaced the retired [[Lee Roy Jordan]] as the team's [[middle linebacker]] and defensive signal caller,<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1734&dat=19771028&id=M1AcAAAAIBAJ&sjid=i1EEAAAAIBAJ&pg=4470,6032293&hl=es | title=Sports in Brief | accessdate=April 13, 2017}}</ref> making him just the third player in franchise history (25 yrs) to hold the position as a regular starter. In [[1979 NFL season|1979]], he registered 18 tackles (9 solo) in one game against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]]. He led the team in tackles in six seasons and broke the Cowboys' single-season tackle record (167) in 1979.

Breunig started 117 straight games, until missing half of the [[1984 NFL season|1984 season]] because of back problems that led to his retirement. He ended his career as the franchise's second-leading tackler (behind Jordan) with 1,016 stops, having played in ten seasons, appearing in 20 playoff games, six [[NFC Championship Game|NFC championships]] and three [[Super Bowl]]s. He was a four-time team captain, a three-time [[Pro Bowl]]er, a second-team [[All-Pro]] and a four-time [[National Football Conference|All-NFC]] selection.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.dallascowboys.com/news/2017/04/13/top-10-nearly-40-combined-pro-bowl-selections-among-best-3rd-round-picks | title=Top 10: Nearly 40 Combined Pro Bowl Selections Among Best 3rd-Round Picks | accessdate=April 13, 2017}}</ref>

Breunig was named to the [[Dallas Cowboys]] ''Ft. Worth Star Telegram'' 50 Year/50 Player Dallas Cowboy Anniversary Team, the 1999 ''Sporting News'' All Time  Dallas Cowboy Team, ''USA Today'' Sports 2014 All Time Dallas Cowboy Defense Team and in 2016 the ''Dallas Morning News'' All Time Top 5 Dallas Cowboy Linebackers.

==Personal life==
After [[American football|football]] he entered into a partnership with former teammate [[Roger Staubach]], in Investment/Development Real Estate. Bob acquired that Company in 1990 and operated a continuing successful venture until 2008 at which time the company was sold and Bob transitioned to other endeavors.

Bob was named the Dallas Father of the Year in 2006 and has been recognized for a number of other civic initiatives and has served on Several Charitable Boards through the years including Fellowship of Christian Athletes, The Urban Alternative, Young Life, Arizona State University Board of Trustees, National Search Ministries, Liberty Institute, Happy Hill Farm Children's Home and Fellowship Bible Church Dallas (Elder).

'''Robert Douglas Christian''' (born November 14, 1968) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Fullback (American football)|fullback]] for 10 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Chicago Bears]], [[Carolina Panthers]], and [[Atlanta Falcons]] from 1992 to 2002. He played [[college football]] for the [[Northwestern Wildcats football|Northwestern Wildcats]] and was selected by the Falcons in the 12th round of the [[1991 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1991 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1991/draft.htm |access-date=May 7, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was also selected by the [[Carolina Panthers]] in the [[1995 NFL expansion draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 16, 1995 |title=NFL Expansion Draft |url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1995/02/16/nfl-expansion-draft/ |access-date=November 2, 2023 |website=Tampa Bay Times |language=en}}</ref>

== College career ==
Christian played [[college football]] for [[Northwestern University]] where he set records (since broken) for career rushing, single season rushing, and single game all-purpose yards.

== Professional career ==
Christian played with [[Chicago Bears]] and [[Carolina Panthers]] prior to signing with [[Atlanta Falcons|Atlanta]] in 1997 and had 831 yards and 12 touchdowns on 193 carries in 135 games, including 85 starts. He had 230 receptions for 2,048 yards and seven touchdowns. Christian retired on March 13, 2003, after 11 seasons in the NFL.

'''Robert Joseph Hallen''' (born March 9, 1975) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive guard]] and [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

Hallen played high school football at [[Mentor High School]], where he was honorable mention all-state his senior season after serving as team captain.  Hallen was a four-year starter playing [[college football]] for the [[Kent State Golden Flashes football|Kent State Golden Flashes]], starting 44 consecutive games. In the spring of 1997, Hallen was awarded the Don Nottingham Cup as the team's top offensive player at the conclusion of Spring practice. He was a first-team All-[[Mid-American Conference]] choice in 1997 after switching to right tackle after three seasons at center. Hallen also served as team captain during the senior year.

Following his senior season, Hallen was chosen to play in the 1998 Senior Bowl in [[Mobile, Alabama]], marking the first time a Kent State player participated in this bowl game. Hallen was selected in the [[1998 NFL draft]] by the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in the second round <ref>{{Cite web |title=1998 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1998/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=pDcxAAAAIBAJ&pg=3827,3913956&dq=football+bob-hallen&hl=en|title=Falcons stay in backyard making Jacket top pick|date=19 April 1998|work=[[Rome News-Tribune]]|publisher=[[Associated Press|AP]]|page=4B|accessdate=15 June 2010}}</ref> (53rd overall) and went on to play in [[Super Bowl XXXIII]].  He played from 1998 to 2001 for the Falcons. He also played for the [[San Diego Chargers]] from 2002 to 2005. He signed with the [[Cleveland Browns]] prior to the [[2006 NFL season]].

Hallen's career came to an end on August 11, 2006, when he announced his retirement due to ongoing problems with his back, which he first injured in the 2001 season while playing for the Falcons.

Hallen announced his retirement shortly after he was named the Browns' starting center in place of injured [[LeCharles Bentley]]. Hallen had left practice several days earlier complaining of back spasms. Hallen notified the Browns of his retirement in a letter.

Hallen was inducted into Mentor High School's Sports Hall Of Fame in 2005 and the Kent State University's Varsity "K" Hall Of Fame in 2014.

Hallen currently works for a fire department in the Greater Cleveland area.

'''Robert Donald Chandler''' (April 24, 1949 – January 27, 1995) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for twelve seasons.<ref name=latobt>{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-01-28-sp-25175-story.html |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |last=Stewart |first=Larry |title=Ex-Raider Bob Chandler is dead at 45 |date=January 28, 1995 |access-date=January 23, 2017}}</ref>

==Early life==
Born in [[Long Beach, California]] in April 1949, Chandler was raised in [[Whittier, California|Whittier]] and graduated from [[Whittier High School]] in 1967. He was considered one of the best all-around high school athletes to play in [[Southern California|southern]] California. He was All-[[California Interscholastic Federation|CIF]] in football and basketball and was one of the country's top high school [[Decathlon|decathletes]], [[High jump|high-jumping]] {{Height|ft=6|in=7}}, [[Pole vault|pole-vaulted]] more than {{convert|13|ft}}, and [[Shot put|put]] the {{convert|12|lb|adj=on}} shot {{convert|57|ft}}.<ref name=latobt/>

==College career==
Chandler played [[college football]] at the [[USC Trojans football|University of Southern California]] in [[Los Angeles]]; he was a [[Captain (sports)|captain]] and the team's leading receiver during his senior year in [[1970 USC Trojans football team|1970]]. He played in two [[Rose Bowl Game|Rose Bowl]] games; as a junior he was named Most Valuable Player of the [[1970 Rose Bowl]]. In the third quarter, Chandler caught a 33-yard touchdown pass from Trojan quarterback [[Jimmy Jones (quarterback)|Jimmy Jones]] and broke several [[1969 Michigan Wolverines football team|Michigan]] tackles to score and gave USC its margin of victory, 10–3.<ref name=winform>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=H6hVAAAAIBAJ&sjid=9OADAAAAIBAJ&pg=6508%2C363489 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon|agency=Associated Press |title=USC's winning Rose Bowl formula: Wild bunch + 1 |date=January 2, 1970 |page=3B }}</ref>

==Professional career==
A [[1971 NFL draft#Round seven|seventh round]] pick in the [[1971 NFL draft]], Chandler played nine seasons with the [[Buffalo Bills]] {{nowrap|(1971–1979)}} and three with the [[Oakland Raiders]] (who moved to Los Angeles by his final playing season) {{nowrap|(1980–1982).}} He led the NFL in receptions from {{nowrap|1975–1977}} with 176, and was named Second-team All-Pro in {{nfly|1975}} and {{nfly|1977}}. He also caught four passes for 77 yards in the [[1980 Oakland Raiders season|Raiders']] 27–10 [[Super Bowl XV]] victory over the [[1980 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] in January 1981.<ref name=tnolft>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=GBBWAAAAIBAJ&sjid=TuIDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6127%2C7011622 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon|agency=Associated Press |title=There's no one left to favor over Raiders |date=January 26, 1981 |page=1D}}</ref>

In the first game of the [[1981 Oakland Raiders season|1981]] season against the [[1981 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]], Chandler stretched out for a pass and took a hit so severe it ruptured his [[spleen]].<ref name=ciacar>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=JoRUAAAAIBAJ&sjid=HI8DAAAAIBAJ&pg=2619%2C7316816 |newspaper=Ellensburg Daily Record |location=Washington|agency=UPI |title=Raiders' Chandler calling it a career |date=July 19, 1983 |page=11}}</ref>  Chandler was rushed to a Denver hospital where doctors saved his life. Chandler made a miraculous recovery and returned to the field later in the season, appearing in a total of eleven regular season games.{{Citation needed|date=January 2008}}. Though he wasn't able to return right away as a receiver, he was able to resume his normal duties holding the ball for Raiders placekicker [[Chris Bahr]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1981/09/17/Fans-attending-Oaklands-regular-season-home-opener-against-Seattle/1552369547200/|title = Fans attending Oakland's regular season home opener against Seattle}}</ref>

In his rookie season of 1971, Chandler saw action in only a handful of games, finishing the season five receptions for 60 yards. Bills coach [[Harvey Johnson (coach)|Harvey Johnson]] was dismissed at the end of the season and the Bills named [[Lou Saban]] as their new head coach. Saban began to use Chandler more in the offense, as Chandler was a starter in all 14 games that season. He scored his first professional touchdown in a 38-14 blow out of the [[New England Patriots]]. The opposing quarterback that day was [[Jim Plunkett]], who would be Chandler's teammate on the Raiders several years later.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/197210080buf.htm|title = New England Patriots at Buffalo Bills - October 8th, 1972|website = [[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]}}</ref> Over the next several seasons for Buffalo, Chandler would be one of the core starters and a favorite target of Bills quarterback [[Joe Ferguson]]. Chandler's role was greatly reduced under coach [[Chuck Knox]] in 1979. Knox preferred a solid ground game over the passing game. In 1980, Chandler was traded to the Raiders for LB [[Phil Villapiano]] and was part of a Raiders team that won Super Bowl XV.

He retired in July 1983;<ref name=ciacar/> for his career, he had 370 receptions for 5,243 yards and 48 touchdowns, along with 11 carries for 18 yards.

Chandler and running back [[O. J. Simpson]] were teammates for a season in college ([[1968 USC Trojans football team|1968]]) and seven in the pros at Buffalo (1971–77).

==Broadcasting career==
Chandler served as a [[color analyst]] for NFL games on [[NFL on NBC|NBC]] in 1983, hosted ''2 On The Town'' for [[KCBS-TV]] in Los Angeles from 1984 to 1987, was a sports reporter for [[KABC-TV]] in the late 1980s and hosted ''Amazing Games'' (a global documentary series about the world's most exotic sports) for [[ESPN]] in 1989. He also served as a "Technical Advisor" for the humor book ''The Unofficial NFL Players Handbook''.

==Personal life==
Chandler's father Gene was the mayor of [[Whittier, California]] from 1987 to 1988. Chandler married his college sweetheart, Marilyn, and had three children: Marisa, Justin, and Emma. Chandler earned a law degree from [[Western State University College of Law]].<ref name="SI">{{Cite magazine |url=https://www.si.com/vault/1982/07/12/625651/the-bare-facts-are-hes-a-star |title=The Bare Facts Are He's A Star |last=Looney |first=Douglas S. |date=July 12, 1982 |magazine=Sports Illustrated |access-date=April 19, 2018}}</ref> Chandler posed for ''[[Playgirl]]'' magazine in January 1982.<ref name="SI"/> Chandler's niece Sarah George Chester and her daughter Payton were two of the nine victims, along with [[Kobe Bryant]] and his 13-year-old daughter [[Gianna Bryant|Gianna]], on board [[2020 Calabasas helicopter crash|the helicopter that crashed]] in [[Calabasas, California]] on January 26, 2020. Chandler's nephew Jake George #81 is a WR for the [[University of Arizona]] Wildcats Football team.

==Death==
Chandler began experiencing a nagging cough in 1994. A rare strain of [[lung cancer]] was discovered in his lungs in September 1994. He continued to work on Raider broadcasts while undergoing chemotherapy treatment at the [[USC Norris Comprehensive Cancer Center|USC Norris Cancer Center]], but died there on Friday, January 27, 1995, at the age of 45, after a four-month battle with cancer.<ref name=latobt/> He was buried at [[Rose Hills Memorial Park]] in Whittier.

==Legacy==
In 1996, USC established the annual Bob Chandler Award, given to an underclassman based on his athletic ability, academic scholarship as well as character on and off the field. The award funds a scholarship for the player's full tuition, room, and board for the following year.

Chandler was inducted into the USC Hall of Fame in November 1999. Highlights of his USC athletic career are on permanent display in USC's Heritage Hall lobby.

Whittier High School's sports facilities are named the Bob Chandler Sports Complex.

Bob was inducted into the Greater Buffalo Sports Hall of Fame in 2023.

'''Robert Anthony Bruer''' (born May 22, 1953) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player and coach.  He played [[tight end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[San Francisco 49ers]] and the [[Minnesota Vikings]] from 1977 until 1985. He played [[college football]] for the [[Mankato State Mavericks football|Mankato State Mavericks]].

==Playing career==
Bruer played for the San Francisco 49ers for one full season, and one game of a second season before being waived by [[Bill Walsh]]. The Minnesota Vikings selected him off waivers shortly after being waived, and he stayed with the Vikings for the remainder of his career. Before the NFL, Bruer played two seasons in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) for the [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]].

Bruer caught [[Joe Montana]]'s first NFL touchdown pass against the Broncos on November 18, 1979.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/score.cgi?type=pass&id=MontJo01 |title=Every Touchdown Thrown by Joe Montana |website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] |access-date=June 20, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303173750/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/score.cgi?type=pass&id=MontJo01 |archive-date=March 3, 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref> It was also Bruer's first NFL touchdown catch, and his only TD with the 49ers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.49ers.com/news/75-for-75-joe-montana-s-first-touchdown-pass |title=75 for 75: Joe Montana's First Touchdown Pass |first=Joe |last=Hession |date=September 24, 2021 |website=49ers.com |access-date=January 28, 2026}}</ref>

==Coaching career==
Bruer later coached football at his alma mater, the [[Minnesota State University, Mankato]].{{Cn|date=February 2025}}

'''Robert Babich'''  (May 5, 1947 – April 4, 2022)<ref>[https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/sports/chargers-rams/story/2022-04-19/former-chargers-linebacker-bob-babich-dies-at-74 Former Chargers linebacker Bob Babich dies at 74]</ref> was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for nine seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[San Diego Chargers]] and the [[Cleveland Browns]]. He played [[college football]] at [[Miami University]] in [[Oxford, Ohio]], and was elected to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] in 1994.<ref name="databasefootball">{{cite web|url=http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=BABICBOB01 |title=Bob Babich Past Stats, Statistics, History, and Awards - databaseFootball.com |publisher=databasefootball.com |access-date=2015-03-02 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150330021610/http://databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=BABICBOB01 |archive-date=2015-03-30 }}</ref>

==Early life==
Babich was born May 5, 1947, the son of Frank Babich, Jr. and mother, Mary (Lisko) Babich.<ref name="wkbn.com">{{cite web | url=https://www.wkbn.com/my-valley-tributes/wasko-funeral-home/robert-bob-babich-campbell-ohio/ | title=Robert "Bob" Babich, Campbell, Ohio | date=8 June 2022 }}</ref> He played high school football for [[Campbell Memorial High School]] in [[Campbell, Ohio]], where he also excelled in baseball.<ref name="wkbn.com"/>

==College career==
Babich decided to play for coach [[Bo Schembechler]] at Miami (Ohio). He was a first-team All-America linebacker for Miami University, known then as the Redskins. He graduated in 1969. He was voted the "Most Valuable Player" award twice by his teammates and selected as Miami's "Athlete of the Year" for the 1968-69 academic year. A two-time unanimous all-[[Mid-American Conference]] linebacker, he was also voted the "Defensive Player of the Year" in the MAC as he captained the 1968 team. Babich was selected First-team All-America by the [[American Football Coaches Association]], ''[[The Sporting News]]'' and ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine. He played in the American, North-South and Senior bowls.<ref name="muredhawks">{{cite web|url=http://www.muredhawks.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=26100&ATCLID=208497060|title=1975 Miami Athletics Hall of Fame Class - MURedHawks.com - The Official Athletic Website of Miami University|publisher=muredhawks.com|access-date=2015-03-02}}</ref>

==Professional career==
He was a first-round draft choice of the San Diego Chargers in the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]], the 18th selection overall and the second linebacker taken.<ref name="footballfoundation">{{cite web|url={{College Football HoF/url|id=1908}}|title=Bob Babich|publisher=footballfoundation.org|access-date=2015-03-02}}</ref>

In three seasons for the Chargers, he saw action in all 42 regular-season games. On September 6, 1973, he was traded to the Cleveland Browns for a first-round draft choice in 1974 and a second-round pick in 1975.<ref name="google">{{cite book|title=Cleveland Browns A-Z|author1=Gordon, R.|author2=Pruitt, M.|date=2002|publisher=Sports Pub|isbn=9781582612409|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iqFHJnbKSOsC|page=9|access-date=2015-03-02}}</ref> He played six seasons for the Browns, missing only three games (in 1975) during those seasons.<ref name="pro-football-reference">{{cite web|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BabiBo20.htm|title=Bob Babich NFL Football Statistics | Pro-Football-Reference.com|publisher=pro-football-reference.com|access-date=2015-03-02}}</ref>

He graduated with a Bachelor of Science in Education.<ref name="wkbn.com"/>

Babich was inducted into the Miami University Athletics Hall of Fame in 1975.<ref name="muredhawks"/> His 1994 election to the College Football Hall of Fame made him the first Miami (Ohio) player to be enshrined.<ref name="footballfoundation"/>

==Personal life==
Babich died on April 3, 2022. His wife, Barbara (Caylor), died just a month earlier.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/sports/chargers-rams/story/2022-04-19/former-chargers-linebacker-bob-babich-dies-at-74 | title=Former Chargers linebacker Bob Babich dies at 74 | date=19 April 2022 }}</ref>

'''Robert Louis Brudzinski''' (born January 1, 1955) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for 13 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL), primarily with the [[Miami Dolphins]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]], earning consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors in 1976.

==Ohio State==
Brudzinski was a four-time letter winner and a three-year starter at [[defensive end]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]]. He was a two-time [[List of All-Big Ten Conference football teams|All-Big Ten Conference]] selection and as a senior in 1976, he was a consensus [[1976 College Football All-America Team|All-America]] choice. In his 43 games for Ohio State he totaled 214 tackles and in 1976 he intercepted four passes, a high number for a defensive end. In 2000 Brudzinski was voted to the [[Ohio State Football All-Century Team]].

== Los Angeles Rams ==
The [[Los Angeles Rams]] drafted Brudzinski with the 23rd pick in the first round of the [[1977 NFL draft]]. The Rams planned moving him to outside linebacker, to match his 4.7 speed and good strength. He started as a rookie because starting middle linebacker [[Jack Reynolds (American football)|Jack Reynolds]] held out for the first one-third of the season. While starting left linebacker [[Jim Youngblood]] moved to the middle to fill in for Reynolds, Brudzinski started at left linebacker. He ended up starting seven games and recording 37 tackles, two interceptions, three forced fumbles and one sack. He was voted All-Rookie by UPI and PFWA and FD for his efforts in 1977. In 1978, he became the starter at right outside linebacker in week 10 when [[Isiah Robertson]] walked out of camp purported with complaints about his salary. The Rams defense was ranked #1 in the NFL at the time and in the {{frac|2|1|2}} months with Brudzinski starting they never fell from the top status. He ended the year with 43 tackles, intercepted a pass that went for a touchdown and two quarterback sacks.

In 1979 Brudzinski had his best year to date. Making all 16 starts as the RLB and being named 2nd-team All-pro by the [[Gannett]] Wire Service. "Bru" as his teammates called him, amassed 127 tackles, with 7 of those for a loss, plus 5 sacks, he intercepted a pass, forced a fumble, recovered one and broke up 14 passes, either at the line of scrimmage or in coverage. The Rams went through the NFC playoffs beating the [[Dallas Cowboys]] and Tampa Bay Buccaneers before losing [[Super Bowl XIV]] to the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]].

Two-thirds into the 1980 season Brudzinski walked out and never returned to the Rams. To date, he had made 35 tackles and had 6 passes defensed plus a sack, but felt he was underpaid. He was replaced by [[George Andrews (American football)|George Andrews]].

The Rams were forced to trade Brudzinski and did so in the spring of 1981. The Rams received multiple picks and the top pick was used to draft future star linebacker [[Jim Collins (linebacker)|Jim Collins]]. With the Rams Brudzinski totaled 242 tackles, 9 sacks, and over 20 passes broken up in his 55 games (41 starts) with the Rams.<ref>1981 Los Angeles Rams Media Guide</ref>

==Miami Dolphins==
Brudzinski played 125 games with 94 starts for [[Don Shula]]'s Dolphins from 1981 though 1989, recording 14{{frac|1|2}} sacks to bring his career total to 23{{frac|1|2}} to go with his nine interceptions.<ref>Pro Football Reference.com</ref>

Brudzinski adapted quickly to the [[Bill Arnsbarger]]-coached defense nicknamed the "Killer-Bs" which propelled the Dolphins to the 1981 playoffs and the 1982 Super Bowl as well as the 1984 Super Bowl.

While with Miami, Brudzinski was voted to the All-Time Dolphins team in the early 2000s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.sun-sentinel.com/sports/sfl-alltimefins-experts,0,2778183.htmlstory |title="Experts All-Time Team" |access-date=2013-09-27 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080918004630/http://www.sun-sentinel.com/sports/sfl-alltimefins-experts%2C0%2C2778183.htmlstory |archive-date=2008-09-18 }} ''Miami Sun-Sentinel''</ref> He was mentioned in articles that ask "Who is the best linebacker never to play in a Pro Bowl?" and Brudzinski's name often comes up since he played well for a long period of time and was never honored by a Pro Bowl selection, even after his stellar 1979 season.

== Bru's Room ==
Founder and owner of Bru's Room Sports Grill.

'''Robert Douglas Johnson''' (born August 19, 1946) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] for 12 seasons with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]], first in the [[American Football League]] (AFL), and then in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]]. Johnson was the [[List of Cincinnati Bengals first-round draft picks|Bengals' first-ever draft selection]] when he was chosen with the [[List of second overall NFL draft picks|second overall pick]] in the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft]].

==College career==
Johnson played [[college football]] at the [[University of Tennessee]], where he was the first recruit of Tennessee coach [[Doug Dickey]]. He was named both [[List of All-SEC football teams|All-Southeastern Conference]] (SEC) and All-American in 1966 and again in 1967. He earned the Jacobs Trophy, given to the SEC's best blocker, and he was named the SEC's Most Outstanding Lineman by the Birmingham Touchdown Club. Johnson finished sixth in the [[Heisman Trophy]] voting as a center.<ref name="BobJohnson">{{Cite web |title=Bob Johnson |url=http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/johnson_bob00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304052418/http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/johnson_bob00.html |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |access-date=January 21, 2014 |website=Tennessee Volunteers Athletics}}</ref>

Also in 1967, he was named an Academic All-American and was vice president of his class while earning a degree in industrial engineering.<ref name="BobJohnson" />

In 1989, he was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bob Johnson (1989) - Hall of Fame |url=https://footballfoundation.org/hof_search.aspx?hof=1900 |access-date=2024-03-17 |website=National Football Foundation |language=en}}</ref>

==Professional career==
He was the first player chosen by the Bengals in their initial season in [[1968 NFL draft|1968]]. He was the second pick overall in the draft, preceded by future Hall of Famer [[Ron Yary]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1968 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1968/draft.htm |access-date=2024-03-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He was the second highest-drafted center ever selected in an NFL Draft, after [[Ki Aldrich]] in [[1939 NFL Draft|1939]].

He was an [[American Football League All-Star games|AFL All-Star]] in [[1968 AFL season|1968]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1968 AFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1968_AFL/probowl.htm |access-date=2024-03-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

Johnson was the last original Bengal to retire, after the 1978 season. His uniform number 54 was retired by the team, and remains the only number the team has retired. However, he came out of retirement in 1979 when Bengals center [[Blair Bush]] suffered a knee injury and the Bengals asked Johnson to return as a long snapper on punts, field goals and extra points.<ref>{{cite web | last=Kirkendall | first=Josh | title=Best Bengals Draft Pick #4: The Original Bengal Bob Johnson | website=Cincy Jungle|publisher=USA Today | date=2011-04-25 | url=https://www.cincyjungle.com/2011/4/25/2132155/best-bengals-draft-pick-4-the-original-bengal-bob-johnson | access-date=2025-07-04}}</ref>

Following his retirement as a player, Johnson worked as a [[color analyst]] on Bengals radio from 1981 to 1985. He also worked as a color analyst on some ESPN college football broadcasts in 1979 prior to his return to the Bengals.

'''Robert Kenneth Heinz''' (born July 25, 1947) is a former [[defensive tackle]] in American college and professional [[American football|football]]. He was drafted in the 2nd round (37th pick overall) of the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]] by the [[Miami Dolphins]], and played professionally for the Miami Dolphins and the [[Washington Commanders|Washington Redskins]].

==Biography==
Heinz was born in [[Milwaukee|Milwaukee, Wisconsin]] and attended [[Messmer High School]] in Milwaukee and [[Lincoln High School (Stockton, California)|Lincoln High School]] in [[Stockton, California]].<ref>{{cite web
 |url=http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=HEINZBOB01
 |title=Bob Heinz
 |publisher=databaseFootball.com
 |accessdate=October 17, 2013
 |url-status=usurped
 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131018014918/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=HEINZBOB01
 |archivedate=October 18, 2013
}}</ref> He played [[college football]] at [[San Joaquin Delta College]]<ref>{{cite web|url= http://californiacommunitycolleges.cccco.edu/Newsroom/NotableAlumni/NFLAlumni.aspx|title= NFL Alumni|publisher= California Community Colleges Chancelor's Office|accessdate= October 17, 2013|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131019045813/http://californiacommunitycolleges.cccco.edu/Newsroom/NotableAlumni/NFLAlumni.aspx|archive-date= October 19, 2013|url-status= dead}}</ref> and the [[University of the Pacific (United States)|University of the Pacific]]. Heinz was inducted into the University of the Pacific Hall of Fame as a 1987-1988 Inductee.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.pacifictigers.com/information/hall_of_fame/all_time/index|title= PACIFIC ATHLETICS HALL OF FAME|publisher=Pacific Tigers |accessdate= October 17, 2013}}</ref>

He played for the Miami Dolphins from 1969 to 1977 and for the Washington Redskins in 1978. He is a member of the [[Perfect season|undefeated]] (17–0) [[1972 Miami Dolphins season|1972 Miami Dolphins]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm2976472/|title=Bob Heinz|website=[[IMDb]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.affinityonline.org/tabid/197/xmmid/833/cat/San%20Joaquin%20Delta%20College/xmview/1/Default.aspx |title= Alumni List |publisher= Affinity Online |accessdate= October 17, 2013 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131019052454/http://www.affinityonline.org/tabid/197/xmmid/833/cat/San%20Joaquin%20Delta%20College/xmview/1/Default.aspx |archive-date= 2013-10-19 |url-status= dead }}</ref>

After retiring from the NFL, Heinz became an advertising executive in [[Palo Alto, California]].<ref>{{cite web|url= http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1997-08-28/sports/9711140267_1_surgery-vern-den-herder-doug-crusan/2|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131018025136/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1997-08-28/sports/9711140267_1_surgery-vern-den-herder-doug-crusan/2|url-status= dead|archive-date= October 18, 2013|title= A Perfect Time To Remember
|publisher=Sun Sentinel |accessdate= October 17, 2013}}</ref>

'''Robert Joseph Hyland''' (born July 21, 1945) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] and center [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] for 11 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Green Bay Packers]], [[Chicago Bears]], [[New York Giants]], and the [[New England Patriots]].  He played [[college football]] for the [[Boston College Eagles football|Boston College Eagles]] and was selected in the first round (ninth overall) of the [[1967 NFL/AFL draft]]. He played high school football at [[Archbishop Stepinac High School|Archbishop Stepinac]] (Class of 1963).

Hyland owned the now-defunct Sports Page pub and Sports Page in White Plains, New York.<ref name="p829">{{cite web | last=Eberhart | first=Christopher J. | title=The last page: Bob Hyland's Sports Page closes for good | website=lohud.com | date=2017-04-08 | url=https://www.lohud.com/story/money/business/2017/04/07/hylands-sports-page-closes/100200350/ | access-date=2025-03-07}}</ref>

In March 2011, Hyland ran as the Republican candidate for mayor of [[White Plains, New York]],<ref>Pellegrin, Michael. [http://whiteplains.patch.com/articles/republicans-announce-hyland-as-their-candidate-for-mayor "Republicans Announce Hyland as Their Candidate for Mayor"], ''White Plains Patch'', March 13, 2011</ref> in the wake of mayor [[Adam Bradley (politician)|Adam Bradley]]'s resignation.<ref>Sciortino, Dina. [http://whiteplains.patch.com/articles/a-brief-on-tuesdays-city-meetings "A Brief on Tuesday’s City Meetings"], ''White Plains Patch'', March 1, 2011</ref> He was defeated by [[Thomas Roach (mayor)|Thomas Roach]].
