[[Dayton Flyers football|Dayton]] (1959–1960) | draftyear = 1960 | draftround = 14 | draftpick = 157 | afldraftyear = 1960 | afldraftround = | pastteams = * [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] ({{NFL Year|1961|1969}}) * [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] (1970)* * [[Miami Dolphins]] ({{NFL Year|1970|1971}}) * [[Cleveland Browns]] ({{NFL Year|1972|1974}}) * [[Los Angeles Rams]] ({{NFL Year|1975}}) | highlights = * First-team [[All-Pro]] ([[1967 All-Pro Team|1967]]) * 2× Second-team All-Pro ([[1963 All-Pro Team|1963]], [[1968 All-Pro Team|1968]]) * 3× [[Pro Bowl]] ([[1964 Pro Bowl|1963]], [[1966 Pro Bowl|1965]], [[1968 Pro Bowl|1967]]) * Third-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] ([[1960 College Football All-America Team|1960]]) | statlabel1 = Games played | statvalue1 = 185 | statlabel2 = Games started | statvalue2 = 163 | statlabel3 = [[Fumble]] recoveries | statvalue3 = 8 | pfr = D/DeMaBo00 }} '''Robert DeMarco''' (born September 16, 1938) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (gridiron football)|center]] for 15 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for four teams. He played [[college football]] for the [[Indiana Hoosiers football|Indiana Hoosiers]] and [[Dayton Flyers football|Dayton Flyers]]. ==Early life== DeMarco was born on September 16, 1938 in [[Jersey City, New Jersey]] to Albert and Louise DeMarco.{{Cite web |last=Moore |first=Tim |title=Bob DeMarco |url=https://www.stlshof.com/bob-demarco/ |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=St Louis Sports Hall of Fame |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |title=Dolores DeMarco Obituary (1931 - 2015) - Wood-Ridge, MO - The Record/Herald News |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/northjersey/name/dolores-demarco-obituary?id=18124942 |access-date=2025-05-06 |website=Legacy.com}} Raised in [[Wood-Ridge, New Jersey]], DeMarco graduated in 1956 from [[St. Mary High School (Rutherford, New Jersey)|St. Mary High School]] in nearby [[Rutherford, New Jersey]], where he played both the offensive and defensive lines on the school's football team. In 1953, the undefeated Gaels won the state championship, his sophomore year.{{Cite news |last=Carroll |first=Mickey |date=November 29, 1954 |title=St. Mary's Beats Lucans In Title Game, 27–6 |work=The Herald-News (Passaic, New Jersey) |pages=23}} The 1953 team was inducted into the St. Mary High School Athletic Hall of Fame in 1997.{{Cite web |title=St. Mary High School Athletic Hall of Fame > Members |url=https://www.stmaryhshof.org/Members.aspx |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=www.stmaryhshof.org}} == College == DeMarco received a football scholarship to [[Indiana Hoosiers football|Indiana University]], where he played one year. He transferred to the [[University of Dayton]] where he played two years, and was team captain his senior year. DeMarco graduated in 1961 with degrees in business management and economics. He was selected to the Kodak All-American Team in 1960, and played in the [[Blue–Gray Football Classic|Blue-Gray Game]] and [[Senior Bowl]] in 1960. He received honorable mention for [[United Press International]]'s (UPI) 1960 All-America team.{{Cite news |last=Peterson |first=Leo H. |date=November 30, 1960 |title=Bellino, Davis, Gibbs On UPI All-America Team |work=The Herald-News (Passaic, New Jersey) |pages=49}} ==Professional career== DeMarco was selected by the [[Chicago Cardinals]] in the 14th round of [[1960 NFL draft]], the 157th overall selection.{{Cite web |title=1960 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1960/draft.htm |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} DeMarco played in the NFL from 1961 to 1969 for the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]], from 1970 to 1971 for the [[Miami Dolphins]], from 1972 to 1974 for the [[Cleveland Browns]] and in 1975 for the [[Los Angeles Rams]]Mills, Ed. [http://archive.northjersey.com/sports/where-are-they-now-former-nfl-star-bob-demarco-of-wood-ridge-1.679237 "Where are they now? Former NFL star Bob DeMarco of Wood-Ridge"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202060737/http://archive.northjersey.com/sports/where-are-they-now-former-nfl-star-bob-demarco-of-wood-ridge-1.679237 |date=2017-02-02 }}, ''[[The Record (Bergen County)]]'', January 28, 2014. Accessed January 25, 2017. "Growing up in Wood-Ridge, DeMarco was a two-way lineman at St. Mary and played as a sophomore on the Gaels' unbeaten nine-win team in 1953. Following graduation from the Rutherford parochial school in 1956, DeMarco went to Indiana University before transferring to Dayton, where he received his Bachelor of Science degree in business management and economics in June 1961."{{Cite web |title=Bob DeMarco Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/D/DeMaBo00.htm |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} He played [[Guard (gridiron football)|guard]] as a rookie, but center for the next 14 years after that.{{Cite web |last=Underwood |first=Bob |date=2019-09-07 |title=The Top 100 St. Louis Football Cardinals (20-11) |url=https://thebigredzone.com/2019/09/07/the-top-100-st-louis-football-cardinals-20-11/ |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=THE BIG RED ZONE |language=en}} During the 1960s he served as a player representative for the union. DeMarco was named to three [[Pro Bowl]]s (1963, 1965, 1967) and one [[Associated Press]] (AP) first-team [[All-Pro]] team (1967) while playing for the Cardinals. The AP recognized him as second team All-Pro in 1963 and 1968, and ''[[The Sporting News]]'' named him first team All-Conference in 1964-1965 and 1967-1969. In 1967, DeMarco was awarded a game ball after playing with a broken wrist and torn rib cartilage. In 1967, three other offensive lineman from the Cardinals, [[Irv Goode]] (left guard), [[Ken Gray (American football)|Ken Gray]] (right guard), and [[Ernie McMillan]] (right tackle), along with Cardinals Hall of Fame tight end [[Jackie Smith]], were all selected to the Pro Bowl.{{Cite web |title=1967 NFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1967/probowl.htm |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} Early in their careers, McMillan and DeMarco served in the military together, and soon after became roommates with the Cardinals, a rare interracial pairing at the time.{{Cite web |date=2024-12-10 |title=Cardinals history loses one of its best at the age of 86: OL Ernie McMillan |url=https://cardswire.usatoday.com/2024/12/10/arizona-cardinals-st-louis-death-ernie-mcmillan/ |access-date=2025-01-26 |website=Cards Wire |language=en-US}} The Cardinals released DeMarco after the 1969 season, after a dispute with head coach [[Charley Winner]], and he was claimed by the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. The Steelers traded DeMarco to the Dolphins before the 1970 season to replace the injured [[Tom Goode (American football)|Tom Goode]].{{Cite news |last=Heeren |first=Dave |date=August 31, 1970 |title=Dolphins Obtain Center Bob DeMarco |work=Fort Lauderdale News |pages=41}}{{Cite news |date=September 1, 1970 |title=Pittsburgh Trades Center Bob DeMarco |work=Winston-Salem Journal |pages=14}} DeMarco started every game at center for the Dolphins 1971 team that went to the [[Super Bowl VI]].{{Cite web |title=1971 Miami Dolphins Roster & Players |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/mia/1971_roster.htm |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} He played in the December 25, 1971 AFC playoff game between the Dolphins and [[Kansas City Chiefs]], which is the longest NFL game in history, lasting 82 minutes and 40 seconds of playing time; though the actual time from the beginning to end of the game was three hours and 18 minutes.{{Cite web |title=Miami Dolphins beat Kansas City Chiefs in NFL's longest game {{!}} December 25, 1971 |url=https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/nfl-longest-game-dolphins-chiefs |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=HISTORY |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=1971 - Dolphins vs. Chiefs, AFC Divisional Playoff - "The NFL's Longest Game", NFL 100 |url=https://www.nfl.com/100/originals/100-greatest/games-18 |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=NFL.com |language=en-US}} In 1972, when future Hall of Fame coach [[Don Shula]] made [[Jim Langer]] the starting center during the preseason, at the suggestion of offensive line coach [[Monte Clark]], DeMarco left training camp for a time as he did not believe he would receive a fair chance to compete for the starting job. The Dolphins had traded Demarco to the [[Buffalo Bills]] but he refused to report, and retired. After missing the first two games of the 1972 season, he agreed to be traded to the [[Cleveland Browns]] in exchange for a draft pick.{{Cite web |last=Meyers |first=Jeff |date=2020-07-03 |title=Bob DeMarco: Tough, Opinionated, Outspoken |url=https://thebigredzone.com/2020/07/03/bob-demarco-tough-opinionated-outspoken/ |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=THE BIG RED ZONE |language=en}}{{cite news|via=newspapers.com|title=Disgruntled DeMarco Traded to the Browns|date=September 27, 1972|newspaper=The Newark Advocate|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/24431734/the_newark_advocate/|page=28|accessdate=2018-10-10}}{{Cite web |last=Habib |first=Hal |date=August 30, 2019 |title=Miami Dolphins: How the late Jim Langer rose from nowhere to surprise Don Shula |url=https://www.palmbeachpost.com/story/sports/nfl/2019/08/30/miami-dolphins-how-late-jim-langer-rose-from-nowhere-to-surprise-don-shula/4325197007/ |access-date=2024-11-26 |website=The Palm Beach Post |language=en-US}} He played in Cleveland for three years, starting 27 games in 1973 and 1974. He was traded to the Los Angeles Rams for the 1975 season, his final year. Rams coach Chuck Knox wanted DeMarco to return, but the 37-year-old DeMarco remembered the advice of Hall of Fame center [[Jim Ringo]], that if your body did not recover from the previous week's game until the day before the next game, it was time to retire. ==Personal life== DeMarco worked as a [[stockbroker]] in St. Louis during the offseason.{{Cite news |last=Long |first=Gary |date=December 10, 1970 |title=Dolphins' Offensive Line: Key to Running |work=The Miami Herald |pages=154}} After retiring, DeMarco returned to St. Louis, where he worked in electronics and finance, and was a long-time salesman for a chemical company.{{Cite web |title=Bob DeMarco |url=https://njsportsheroes.com/bobdemarcofb.html |access-date=2025-05-06 |website=njsportsheroes.com}} He was inducted into the St. Louis Sports Hall of Fame in 2018. ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Chicago Cardinals 1960 draft navbox}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Demarco, Bob}} [[Category:1938 births]] [[Category:Living people]] [[Category:American football centers]] [[Category:St. Louis Cardinals (football) players]] [[Category:Cleveland Browns players]] [[Category:Miami Dolphins players]] [[Category:Los Angeles Rams players]] [[Category:Eastern Conference Pro Bowl players]] [[Category:Dayton Flyers football players]] [[Category:Indiana Hoosiers football players]] [[Category:People from Wood-Ridge, New Jersey]] [[Category:Players of American football from Bergen County, New Jersey]] [[Category:Players of American football from Jersey City, New Jersey]] [[Category:St. Mary High School (Rutherford, New Jersey) alumni]]

He played [[college football]] for the [[University of Notre Dame]], and twice earned consensus [[All-American]] honors.{{cite web|title=43 BOB CRABLE|url=http://www.und.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/bob_crable_135542.html|website=UND.com|access-date=1 May 2018}} A first-round pick in the [[1982 NFL draft]], he played professionally for the NFL's [[New York Jets]]. ==Early life== Crable was born in [[Cincinnati, Ohio]], and grew up in nearby [[Deer Park, Ohio|Deer Park]], a Cincinnati suburb. '''Robert Paul Brunet''' (July 29, 1946 – June 26, 2025) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for the [[Washington Commanders|Washington Redskins]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Louisiana Tech Bulldogs football|Louisiana Tech Bulldogs]] and was selected in the seventh round of the [[1968 NFL/AFL draft]].

== College career ==
Brunet led the Bulldogs in rushing in 1965 with 477 yards and again in 1967 with 631 yards, earning all-conference honors in each of those season (a foot injury sidelined Brunet for all of 1966). Over the course of his college career he had five 100-yard-plus games, including a 224-yard effort against Lamar in 1967.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Football Record Book |url=https://latechsports.com/sports/2018/7/20/_m_footbl_media_guides_html.aspx |access-date=2025-07-08 |website=LA Tech Athletics |language=en}}</ref> 

== NFL career ==
As a rookie for the Redskins in 1968, Brunet was Washington's second-leading rusher with 227 yards. He also caught 18 passes for 160 yards and a touchdown. As a pro player, he was used primarily on special teams, appearing overall in 81 games over eight seasons--not including the 1969 he sat out and 1974 he missed due to injuries.<ref>{{Cite book |last= |url=http://archive.org/details/redskins-1975-media-guide-washington-c |title=Washington Redskins 1975 Media Guide |date=}}</ref> Brunet retired after suffering a career-ending injury during the 1977 season.<ref>{{Cite book |last= |url=http://archive.org/details/redskins-1978-media-guide-washington-cbd |title=Washington Redskins 1978 Media Guide |date=}}</ref> 

== Business career ==
In 1973, Brunet and his brother, Billy, began a seafood delivery business in [[Baton Rouge, Louisiana]]. They then turned the company into a restaurant, which opened in 1977 under the name The Galley before being renamed to Brunet's Cajun Restaurant in the early 1980s. They retired in 2011 and closed the restaurant.<ref name = Griggs>{{cite news|url = https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/business/brunet-s-to-close-owners-to-retire/article_68062619-b6cc-5181-ae23-9758fd4b339f.html|title = Brunet's to close; owners to retire|newspaper = [[The Advocate (Louisiana)|The Advocate]]|location = Baton Rouge, Louisiana|last = Griggs|first = Ted|date = August 10, 2011|accessdate = April 9, 2023}}</ref>

== Personal life and death ==
In 2022, Brunet was inducted into the Bayou Region Athletic Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bayou Region Hall of Fame |url=https://www.tghealthsystem.com/news/2022/january/2022-bayou-region-athletic-hall-of-fame-inductee/ |access-date=2025-07-08 |website=Terrebonne General Health System |language=en}}</ref>

Brunet died on June 26, 2025, at the age of 78.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Robert Paul Brunet|url=https://obituaries.theadvocate.com/obituary/robert-brunet-1092974266 |access-date=2025-07-08 |website=The Advocate |language=en}}</ref>

'''Robert Charles Holly, Jr.''' (born June 1, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Washington Redskins]], [[Philadelphia Eagles]] and [[Atlanta Falcons]].  He played [[college football]] for the [[Princeton Tigers football|Princeton Tigers]].<ref>The Football Encyclopedia, St. Martin's Press, 1994, {{ISBN|0-312-11435-4}}</ref>

Born and raised in [[Clifton, New Jersey]], Holly attended [[Clifton High School (New Jersey)|Clifton High School]].<ref>[https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HollBo00.htm Bob Holly Stats], [[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]. Accessed March 14, 2018.</ref>

He attracted the attention of NFL scouts at [[Princeton University]] in 1981 when he set a school record by throwing for 501 yards against Yale, and scoring the go-ahead touchdown on a keeper himself late in the game in a 35–31 victory,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.princeton.edu/football/pfball.html |title=Princeton Football Timeline |access-date=2010-01-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090713014942/http://www.princeton.edu/football/pfball.html |archive-date=2009-07-13 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Princeton's first over arch-rival Yale since 1966.  That year, he set a school record (since broken) by throwing for 2,668 yards, and was named first-team All-Ivy.<ref>GoPrincetonTigers.com ({{cite web |url=http://www.goprincetontigers.com/ |title=Archived copy |accessdate=2012-01-25 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222093448/http://www.goprincetontigers.com//pdf4/380603.pdf?DB_OEM_ID=10600 |archivedate=2015-12-22 }}/pdf7/135152.pdf?SPSID=54345&SPID=4263&DB_OEM_ID=10600)</ref>

He was drafted in the 11th round by the Redskins in 1982, and served as the backup to [[Joe Theismann]] that season, in which the Redskins won the Super Bowl.  He played in 5 regular season games for the Redskins in 1983, completing his only pass attempt, and he appeared in one playoff game, completing the two passes he attempted.<ref>The Football Encyclopedia, St. Martin's Press, 1994, {{ISBN|0-312-11435-4}}</ref>

He was a member of the Philadelphia Eagles and Atlanta Falcons in 1984, but did not appear in any games.  He played in four games for the Falcons in 1985, completing 24 of 39 passes for 295 yards and one touchdown.<ref>The Football Encyclopedia, St. Martin's Press, 1994, {{ISBN|0-312-11435-4}}</ref>

He was injured in a car accident in the off-season after the 1985 season, and retired from pro football.

(April 2, 1946 – September 22, 2020) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played for the [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] (1968–1969) and for the [[Houston Oilers]] (1970–1976). He was born on April 2, 1946, in [[Modesto, California]], and became a native of [[Atlanta, Georgia]]. When he was three years old, his parents, U.S. Navy Sailor Robert and Mary Brown Atkins, relocated their family from California to Georgia in 1949. At Luther J. Price High School, he was an exceptional player in three sports, baseball, basketball, and football. After graduating in 1964, Atkins attended Grambling College—now [[Grambling State University]]—in [[Grambling, Louisiana]]. He received a Bachelor of Science degree in Physical Education and Recreation in 1972. In 1986, he received a Master of Education degree from [[Prairie View A&M University]] (PVAMU) in [[Prairie View, Texas]]. In 1968, the St. Louis Cardinals drafted Atkins in the second round as a cornerback. After the draft, he played in two major all-star games: January 1968, the 19th Annual Senior Bowl All Star Game, and in August 1968, the College All-Star Game against the National Football League World Champs Green Bay Packers. As a rookie with the Cardinals, Atkins became known for his exceptional speed and his authoritative hits. Playing two years for the Cardinals, Atkins was traded to the Houston Oilers in 1970. During his seven-year tenure with the Oilers, he was respected on and off the field for his achievements. He won numerous game balls for outstanding game performances often cited in national and local media. Retiring from the Houston Oilers in 1976, Atkins pursued other opportunities. In 1983, he became Head Women's Basketball Coach and Assistant Football Coach at Sam Houston High School in [[Houston|Houston, Texas]]. Atkins accepted in 1984 the first of three major positions that he would hold at PVAMU: He was the Assistant Football Coach and Head Women's Basketball Coach. Atkins resigned in 2005 from these positions and assumed the position of Director of Athletic Operations. He retired from PVAMU in August 2011. Atkins received recognition from Houston's Third-Ward Community for his exemplary volunteer service rendered to the Professional United Leadership League (PULL). He worked seven years at PULL with inner-city teens for whom he was a big brother and counselor. He received the “L. J. Price School Athletic Alumni Award” at the school's 2009 Second Annual Crimson Award Ceremony held in Atlanta, Georgia. He was commended for scholarly presentations in his fields of expertise at both state and national levels. He was also a member of the NFL Association. On July 8, 2017, Atkins was inducted into the Grambling Legends Hall of Fame. Atkins first marriage was to Norma Jo Wheeler. They had a son, Christopher E. Atkins. Atkins has four grandchildren; Tobias, Simeon, Moorea, and Harysn. Atkins second marriage was to Dottie Winchester Malone Atkins. Atkins died on September 22, 2020, at the age of 74.[https://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2020/09/22/former-oilers-defensive-back-bob-atkins-dies-at-74/ Former Oilers defensive back Bob Atkins dies at 74] ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== *[http://www.nfl.com/players/bobatkins/profile?id=ATK415288 NFL.com player page] *{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20160411193537/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=ATKINBOB01 Football Database page]}} *[http://www.booksamillion.com/p/Grambling-State-University-Alumni/Source-Wikipedia/9781156682432 Grambling State University Alumni Book] {{St. Louis Cardinals 1968 draft navbox}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Atkins, Bob}} [[Category:1946 births]] [[Category:2020 deaths]] [[Category:Players of American football from Atlanta]] [[Category:Players of American football from Modesto, California]] [[Category:American football defensive backs]] [[Category:Grambling State Tigers football players]] [[Category:St. Louis Cardinals (football) players]] [[Category:Houston Oilers players]] [[Category:American women's basketball coaches]] [[Category:20th-century American sportsmen]]

'''Robert Juan Hoskins''' (September 16, 1945 – June 8, 1980) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[San Francisco 49ers]] in the 16th round of the [[1969 NFL/AFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Wichita State Shockers football|Wichita State Shockers]].

Hoskins was born to a large family, having nine siblings. He attended high school in Edwardsville, lettering in football, baseball, and track. He received a scholarship to Wichita State, where he played for two years as a fullback and defensive end. He left the university due to family obligations before completing his eligibility.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Newhouse |first1=Dave |title=Medics Call Signals as Hoskins Gains Yardage Against Cancer |publisher=The Sporting News |date=1974-02-16}}</ref>

In 1969, he played minor league football for the Seattle Rangers of the [[Continental Football League]] (COFL), where he earned all-league honors as a defensive lineman. A tryout in the [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL) was unsuccessful, however in the spring of 1969, he was drafted by the 49ers.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Newhouse |first1=Dave |title=Medics Call Signals as Hoskins Gains Yardage Against Cancer|publisher=The Sporting News |date=1974-02-16}}</ref>

Hoskins suffered injuries and saw little playing time in his first two seasons. However, playing on special teams in the 1971 NFC divisional playoff against the [[Washington Redskins]], he recovered a mis-snapped ball in the end zone, in what proved to be the winning touchdown.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Guback |first1=Steve |title=A Fumble, An Interception, A Bad Snap | publisher=The Evening Star |date=1971-12-27}}</ref> Hoskins started all 14 games the next four seasons.

In 1974, in the midst of his career, Hoskins was diagnosed with [[Hodgkin's Disease]] and underwent treatment. This included two surgeries followed by [[cobalt therapy]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Newhouse |first1=Dave |title=Medics Call Signals as Hoskins Gains Yardage Against Cancer |publisher=The Sporting News |date=1974-02-16}}</ref> Nonetheless, he was able to remain a starter until his retirement at age 30 after the 1975 season.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bob Hoskins |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HoskBo20.htm |website=Pro Football Reference |access-date=2022-07-31}}</ref>

He died of a heart attack in 1980.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Butchock |first1=Steve |title=Sports Today |publisher=The Evening Star |date=1980-06-10}}</ref>

'''Robert Henry Kohrs''' (born November 8, 1958) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a  [[defensive back]] and [[linebacker]] for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Arizona State Sun Devils]] before being selected in the second round of the [[1980 NFL draft]].

==Football career==
Kohrs was born and raised in [[Phoenix, Arizona|Phoenix]]. He had an outstanding high school career at [[Brophy College Preparatory]] and was recruited to play for the [[Arizona State Sun Devils football|Sun Devils]] in 1976. With Arizona State Kohrs racked up 214 tackles and 30 [[quarterback]] sacks. In 1977, he helped the Sun Devils clinch a half-share of the WAC title and berth in the Fiesta Bowl. The next season, in a game against new Pac-10 rival USC, then ranked second in the nation, Kohrs racked up six tackles, including a sack, three fumble recoveries, and three pass deflections, earning himself "Player of the week" honors from ''Sports Illustrated'' magazine. Later in the 1978 campaign, Kohrs had 15 tackles in a game against Arizona. Kohrs made first-team [[Pac-10 Conference|All-Pac-10]] in 1979. He was selected in the 2nd round of the 1980 NFL Draft by the Pittsburgh Steelers. He played five seasons in the NFL before retiring after the 1985 season.

'''Robert Vincent Jury''' (born October 5, 1955) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Safety (American football position)|safety]] for one season with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected by the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in the third round of the [[1978 NFL draft]]. He  played [[college football]] for the [[Pittsburgh Panthers football|Pittsburgh Panthers]].

==Early life==
Robert Vincent Jury was born on October 5, 1955, in [[Los Angeles, California]].<ref name="Pfa">{{cite web | url=http://www.profootballarchives.com/players/j/jury00200.html | title=Bob Jury | publisher=Pro Football Archives | accessdate=26 December 2024}}</ref> He attended [[South Park High School (South Park, Pennsylvania)|South Park High School]] in [[South Park, Pennsylvania]].<ref name="Pfa"/>

==College career==
He was a member of the [[Pittsburgh Panthers football|Pittsburgh Panthers]] from  1974 to 1977 and a three-year [[letterman (sports)|letterman]] from 1975 to 1977.<ref name="Pfa"/><ref>{{cite news | url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2002&dat=19781124&id=dxwvAAAAIBAJ&sjid=jdsFAAAAIBAJ&pg=1388,5806415 | title=Bob Jury finally gets to play with Steelers | work=Beaver County Times | date=November 24, 1978 | accessdate=23 August 2014}}</ref> He led the country with ten interceptions in 1976,<ref name="Sr">{{cite web | url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/bob-jury-1.html?__hstc=223721476.cf5f44155f2e36f92dc58b684a6e9a44.1694291523663.1735254142844.1735258872049.1012&__hssc=223721476.1.1735258872049&__hsfp=3542455373 | title=Bob Jury | publisher=sports-reference.com | accessdate=26 December 2024}}</ref> earning [[Associated Press]] (AP) third-team [[All-American]] and AP and [[United Press International]] (UPI) first-team All-East honors.<ref name=AP>{{cite news|title=Tony Dorsett tops AP All-American Team|newspaper=Jefferson City Post Tribune|date=December 2, 1976|page=13|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/4499583/tony_dorsett_tops_ap_all_american_team/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Dorsett Leads Pitt Plunder Of All-East Votes|newspaper=Observer-Reporter|date=December 15, 1976|page=D-4|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VOZdAAAAIBAJ&dq=1976+All-East+football+team+second&pg=PA44&article_id=1285,2353938}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Pitt Places Seven On All-East Team|newspaper=York Daily Record|date=December 1, 1976|page=16|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/106298937/pitt-places-seven-on-all-east-team/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> The [[1976 Pittsburgh Panthers football team|1976 Panthers]] were named consensus national champions. He made six interceptions for 111 yards his senior year in 1977,<ref name="Sr"/> garnering consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] and AP and UPI first-team All East recognition.<ref name=AW>{{cite web|title=2014 NCAA Football Records: Consensus All-America Selections|publisher=National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA)|year=2014|accessdate=August 16, 2014|page=6|url=http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/stats/football_records/2014/Awards.pdf|archive-date=November 26, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181126094941/http://fs.ncaa.org/Docs/stats/football_records/2014/awards.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/bob-jury-1.html | title=Bob Jury | publisher=Sports Reference LLC | work=sports-reference.com | accessdate=23 August 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Five Repeaters Heading Up AP All-East Football Team|newspaper=The Courier-Express|date=December 1, 1977|page=19|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/106301368/five-repeaters-heading-up-ap-all-east/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Pagliaro, Carfora on All-East squad|newspaper=The Morning Record and Journal|date=November 29, 1977|page=10|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LJ5HAAAAIBAJ&dq=1977+All-East+football+team+upi&pg=PA6&article_id=1694,4965942}}</ref> He is the Panthers' all-time leader in career [[interception]]s (21), interceptions in a season (10) and interception return yards (266).<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.pittsburghpanthers.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/052306aaa.html | title=Bob Jury, 1977 | publisher=pittsburghpanthers.com | accessdate=23 August 2014 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117033414/http://www.pittsburghpanthers.com/sports/m-footbl/spec-rel/052306aaa.html | archive-date=17 November 2015 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Professional career==
Jury was selected by the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in the third round, with the 63rd overall pick, of the [[1978 NFL draft]].<ref name="Pfr">{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/J/JuryBo20.htm | title=Bob Jury | publisher=Pro Football Reference | accessdate=26 December 2024}}</ref> He officially signed with the team on July 5, 1978.<ref name="transactions"/>

On August 29, 1978, Jury and a 1979 third round draft pick were traded to the [[San Francisco 49ers]] for a 1979 third round pick.<ref name="transactions"/><ref>{{cite web | url=https://prosportstransactions.com/football/Search/SearchResults.php?Player=Bob+Jury&Team=&BeginDate=&EndDate=&PlayerMovementChkBx=yes&submit=Search | title=Search Results | publisher=prosportstransactions.com | accessdate=26 December 2024}}</ref> He played in 15 games, starting eight, for the 49ers during the 1978 season, recording one sack and three fumble recoveries.<ref name="Pfr"/> The next year, he was placed on injured reserve on August 23, 1979, and spent the entire season there.<ref name="transactions"/> He was released by the 49ers on January 7, 1980.<ref name="transactions"/>

Jury was claimed off waivers by the [[New York Giants]] on January 16, 1980, but was later waived.<ref name="transactions"/>

He was claimed off waivers by the [[New England Patriots]] on May 19, 1980.<ref name="transactions"/> He was released by the Patriots on July 23, 1980, after leaving the team.<ref name="transactions">{{cite web | url=http://www.profootballarchives.com/transactions/j/jury00200.html | title=Bob Jury NFL Transactions | publisher=Pro Football Archives | accessdate=26 December 2024}}</ref>

'''Robert Hamm''' (born April 24, 1959) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for four seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) with the [[Houston Oilers]], [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and [[Indianapolis Colts]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Nevada Wolf Pack football|Nevada Wolf Pack]].

==Early life and college==
Robert Hamm was born on April 24, 1959, in [[Kansas City, Missouri]].<ref name="Pfa">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/players/h/hamm00200.html | title=Bob Hamm | publisher=Pro Football Archives | accessdate=18 December 2024}}</ref> He attended [[Saint Francis High School (Mountain View)|Saint Francis High School]] in [[Mountain View, California]].<ref name="Pfa"/>

Hamm attended the [[University of Nevada, Reno]], where he was a member of the [[Nevada Wolf Pack football|Wolf Pack]] from 1979 to 1982. He was a [[letterman (sports)|letterman]] in 1980 and 1982.<ref name="Pfa"/>

==Professional career==
After going undrafted in the [[1983 NFL draft]], Hamm signed with the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] on May 9, 1983.<ref name="transactions">{{cite web | url=https://www.profootballarchives.com/transactions/h/hamm00200.html | title=Bob Hamm NFL Transactions | publisher=Pro Football Archives | accessdate=18 December 2024}}</ref> He was waived on August 29, 1983.<ref name="transactions"/>

Hamm was claimed off waivers by the [[Houston Oilers]] on August 30, 1983.<ref name="transactions"/> He played all 16 games during his rookie season in 1983, starting 12 after replacing [[Malcolm Taylor (American football)|Malcolm Taylor]], and recorded three sacks.<ref name="Pfr"/><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1983/10/22/The-presence-of-Bob-Hamm-in-the-starting-lineup/1169435643200/ | title=The presence of Bob Hamm in the starting lineup... | work=[[United Press International]] | date=October 22, 1983 | accessdate=18 December 2024}}</ref> He was placed on injured reserve the next year on August 28, 1984.<ref name="transactions"/> He was activated on September 28 and started the final 12 games of the 1984 season, totaling two sacks and one fumble recovery.<ref name="transactions"/><ref name="Pfr"/>

On April 30, 1985, the Oilers traded Hamm and a 1986 fourth round draft pick to the Chiefs for a 1985 fifth round pick, 1985 sixth round pick, and a 1986 conditional pick.<ref name="transactions"/><ref>{{cite web | url=https://prosportstransactions.com/football/Search/SearchResults.php?Player=Bob+Hamm&Team=&BeginDate=&EndDate=&PlayerMovementChkBx=yes&submit=Search | title=Search Results | publisher=prosportstransactions.com | accessdate=18 December 2024}}</ref> Hamm played in 14 games, starting five, for the Chiefs during the 1985 season and made one sack before being placed on injured reserve on December 11, 1985.<ref name="transactions"/><ref name="Pfr">{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/H/HammBo20.htm | title=Bob Hamm | publisher=Pro Football Reference | accessdate=18 December 2024}}</ref> He was placed on injured reserve again on August 25, 1986, and was later released on November 4, 1986.<ref name="transactions"/>

Hamm signed with the [[New York Jets]] on March 26, 1987.<ref name="transactions"/> He was released on June 10, 1987.<ref name="transactions"/>

On September 23, 1987, Hamm signed with the [[Indianapolis Colts]] during the [[1987 NFL players strike]].<ref name="transactions"/> He appeared in three games for the Colts that season.<ref name="Pfr"/> He was released on October 20, 1987, after the strike ended.<ref name="transactions"/> He later signed a futures contract with the Colts on December 10, 1987,  but retired on July 31, 1988.<ref name="transactions"/>

'''Robert John Brotzki''' (born December 24, 1962) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Indianapolis Colts]] and the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Syracuse Orange football|Syracuse Orange]].

==Early life==
Brotzki attended [[St. Mary Central Catholic High School]] in [[Sandusky, Ohio]], where he played as a [[tight end]]. He received All-state honors as a senior. He accepted a football scholarship from [[Syracuse University]].

As a freshman, he was named the starter at [[tight end]]. He was limited with an injury for most of the season, while finishing fifth on the team with 15 receptions for 131 yards and no [[touchdown]]s. As a junior, he was switched to the [[offensive line]] and was named the starter at [[left tackle]]. He recorded 45 consecutive starts during his college career.

==Professional career==
===Indianapolis Colts===
Brotzki was selected by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in the ninth round (228th overall) of the [[1986 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1986 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1986/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-03 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> As a rookie, he was moved to [[offensive guard]], before being placed on the [[injured reserve list]] with a back injury on August 29.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/106220357/ | title=Colt Notes | accessdate=April 30, 2020}}</ref> He was activated on November 7. He appeared in 2 games as a backup.

In [[1987 NFL season|1987]], he was moved in [[Training camp (National Football League)|training camp]] to [[left tackle]], while [[Chris Hinton]]'s recovered from the arthroscopic knee surgery he had in June.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/105940164/ | title=Colts looking to beat up on Lions Tonight | accessdate=April 30, 2020}}</ref> He also was tried at [[Center (gridiron football)|center]]. He missed the season opener and games from weeks 3 through 5.

In [[1988 NFL season|1988]], he was a backup [[offensive tackle]] in [[Training camp (National Football League)|training camp]], before announcing his retirement. He re-signed with the team on September 22.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/105950743/ | title=Transactions | accessdate=April 30, 2020}}</ref> He played in one game before being waived on September 28, to make room for guard [[Ron Solt]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1988&dat=19880929&id=wGciAAAAIBAJ&sjid=9KwFAAAAIBAJ&pg=4002,2608946&hl=es | title=Transactions | accessdate=April 30, 2020}}</ref>

===Dallas Cowboys===
On October 19, [[1988 NFL season|1988]], he was signed by the [[Dallas Cowboys]]. He appeared in 7 games and was declared inactive for 2 contests.

===Atlanta Falcons===
On February 21, [[1989 NFL season|1989]], he was signed in [[Plan B free agency]] by the [[Atlanta Falcons]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1876&dat=19890222&id=U24sAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Us4EAAAAIBAJ&pg=5090,2389323&hl=es | title=Falcons Sign Brotzki | accessdate=April 30, 2020}}</ref> He was released on September 4.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=348&dat=19890905&id=9WUvAAAAIBAJ&sjid=lDUDAAAAIBAJ&pg=6338,926707&hl=es | title=Falcons Keep 4 Free Agents On Roster | accessdate=April 30, 2020}}</ref>

==Personal life==
After football, he was the [[tight end]] assistant football coach for two years (2007-2008) at [[Robert Morris College]]. In 2009, he was the Director of Player Development at [[Syracuse University]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://cnycentral.com/sports/college/marrone-hires-brotzki-as-director-of-player-development?id=278068| title=Marrone hires Brotzki as director of player development | accessdate=April 30, 2020}}</ref> From 2010 to 2015, he was the Assistant Athletics Director for Player Development.

'''Robert Thomas Jones''' (born September 3, 1978) is an American [[American football|football]] former [[long snapper/defensive line]] in the [[National Football League]] for the [[New York Giants]].

==Football career==
Jones played football at [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State]] from 1998–2001 as a [[defensive lineman]], being named a starter in each of those years.<ref>{{cite web |title=1998 Penn State Nittany Lions Roster |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/penn-state/1998-roster.html |website=College Football Reference |access-date=20 October 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=2001 Penn State Nittany Lions Roster |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/penn-state/2001-roster.html |website=College Football Reference |access-date=20 October 2018}}</ref> He went undrafted in the [[2002 NFL draft]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://games.crossfit.com/article/giving-everything-bobby-jones|title=Giving Everything: Bobby Jones|website=CrossFit Games|first=Brittney|last=Saline|date=March 17, 2014|access-date=February 22, 2026}}</ref>

He eventually signed with the [[New York Giants]], and was named the starting [[long snapper]] for the 2002 season. He performed the Giants' long snapping duties for the first 11 games of the [[2002 NFL season]] before a botched snap leading to a safety and eventual loss to the [[Houston Texans]] resulted in his release.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Anderson |first1=Dave |title=Sports of The Times; Biggest Embarrassment Ever for Giants |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/11/25/sports/sports-of-the-times-biggest-embarrassment-ever-for-giants.html |access-date=20 October 2018 |work=The New York Times |date=November 25, 2002}}</ref>

'''Robert Lee Gregor''' (born February 10, 1957) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive back]] for the [[San Diego Chargers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Washington State Cougars football|Washington State Cougars]]. He was selected by the Chargers in the fourth round of the [[1980 NFL draft]]. After missing the 1980 season while on the [[injured reserve list]], the hard-hitting Gregor [[starting lineup|started]] for San Diego the following three seasons, but he was sidelined by injuries each year.

==Early life==
Gregor was born on February 10, 1957, in [[Riverside, California]]. He attended [[Monte Vista High School (Danville, California)|Monte Vista High School]] in [[Danville, California|Danville]],<ref name=ta_08301984>{{cite news|title=Bob Gregor No. 43|date=August 30, 1984|newspaper=Times-Advocate|at=sec. North County Consumer News, p. 18|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/136145590/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 3, 2023}}</ref> where he played football as a [[flanker (American football)|flanker]], [[cornerback]] and [[punter (gridiron football)|punter]],<ref>{{cite news|first=Alan|last=McCallaster|title=The Defensive Backs Will Be Busy|date=October 22, 1977|newspaper=Oakland Tribune|page=35-E|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/oakland-tribune/136147575/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 4, 2023}}</ref> and was named the team's [[most valuable player]].<ref name=zupan_08241978/> He also excelled in [[basketball]] and [[track and field]],<ref name=zupan_08241978>{{cite news|first=Dan|last=Zupan|title=Walden Plans On Staying|date=August 24, 1978|newspaper=Contra Costa Times|page=29|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/contra-costa-times/136147306/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 3, 2023}}</ref> earning all-league honors in the [[100-yard dash]] and starring as a [[triple jump]]er.<ref name=missildine_11081979/>

==College career==
Gregor was [[college recruiting|recruited]] to [[Washington State University]] by [[Washington State Cougars football|Cougars football]] head coach [[Jim Sweeney (American football, born 1929)|Jim Sweeney]]. Gregor spent five years with the Cougars, missing one season with injuries.<ref name=missildine_11081979/> A tough player, he played aggressively and sometimes recklessly.<ref>{{cite news|first=Don|last=Norcross|title=Chargers' Gregor is accustomed to underdog role|date=July 20, 1980|newspaper=Times-Advocate|page=B-3|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/136147977/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 2, 2023}}</ref> As a fifth-year [[senior (education)|senior]] in 1979, Gregor was called "one of the hardest hitters in this game", by [[Jim Walden (American football)|Jim Walden]], who by then was the Cougars' head coach.<ref name=missildine_11081979/> "Reckless, his hits hurt—sometimes himself", added the coach.<ref name=missildine_11081979>{{cite news|first=Harry|last=Missildine|date=November 8, 1979|title=Bob Gregor: his hits hurt|newspaper=The Spokesman-Review|page=34|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-spokesman-review/136140842/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 2, 2023}}</ref> According to Walden, "only injuries" prevented Gregor from being one of the top players in the [[Pac-10 Conference]].<ref>{{cite news|first=Harry|last=Missildine|title=Sixteen Coug seniors to battle the Huskies|date=November 15, 1979|newspaper=The Spokesman-Review|page=38|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-spokesman-review/136140897/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 2, 2023}}</ref>

==Professional career==
The [[San Diego Chargers]] selected Gregor with their second pick of the [[1980 NFL draft]], choosing him in the fourth round with the 108th overall pick.<ref name=norcross_11241980/><ref>{{cite web|title=Bob Gregor|website=Pro-Football-Reference.com|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GregBo20.htm|accessdate=November 3, 2019}}</ref> The Chargers had him rated as the top [[strong safety]] and 28th best player in the draft,<ref>{{cite news|first=Jerry|last=Magee|title=Quarterback Rich Chargers Pick Up Another|date=April 30, 1980|newspaper=The San Diego Union|page=C-1|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-13CE509D1F92557B@2444360-13CE4F5560C47673@34-13CE4F5560C47673@?search_terms=|via=NewsBank|url-access=subscription|access-date=December 3, 2023}}</ref> which was counter to the NFL trend of valuing a defender's coverage skills over their hitting ability.<ref>{{cite news|first=Jerry|last=Magee|title=Chargers Hopefuls Not Lacking Talent|date=July 29, 1980|newspaper=The San Diego Union|page=C-2|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-13CA694F748A5C2B@2444450-13C8B06051B8D54C@23-13C8B06051B8D54C@|url-access=subscription|via=NewsBank|access-date=December 6, 2023}}</ref> However, he was placed on [[injured reserve]] before the [[1980 San Diego Chargers season|1980 season]] began due to shoulder and ankle injuries.<ref name=norcross_11241980/><ref name=shaw_09101983/> San Diego head coach [[Don Coryell]] said that Gregor hit "so hard I don't know if [he] can last.<ref>{{cite news|first=Dave|last=Distel|title=Experience Wasn't LAsting For Mitchell|date=August 27, 1980|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|at=pt. 4]|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times/136148571/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 6, 2023}}</ref> Later, the team wanted to add him to their active roster midseason, but he would have needed to be placed on [[Waivers (NFL)|waivers]], which Coryell said would be too risky, believing another club would claim him.<ref name=norcross_11241980>{{cite the [[Super Bowl]] that season, losing to [[Oakland Raiders|Oakland]] in the [[AFC Championship Game]].<ref name=norcross_07191981>{{cite news|first=Don|last=Norcross|title=Pardee's task: put Chargers in Super Bowl XVI|date=July 19, 1981|newspaper=Times-Advocate|page=[https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/136310021/ B1], [https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/136310054/ [[File:Bob Gregor.jpg|thumb|left|Gregor against [[Billy Sims]] ''(holding ball)'' and the [[Detroit Lions]] in 1981]]
Looking to improve their defense and reach the Super Bowl, San Diego hired [[Jack Pardee]] in [[1981 San Diego Chargers season|1981]] as its new assistant head coach in charge of their defense.<ref name=norcross_07191981/> Renowned for using a variety of coverages, he replaced defensive coordinator [[Jackie Simpson (linebacker)|Jackie Simpson]], whose defense was criticized for being predictable.<ref name=norcross_07191981/><ref name=distel_09051981/><ref>{{cite news|first=Dave|last=Distel|title=Will This Be the Year?|date=September 3, 1981|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|at=part IX, pp. [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times/136314643/ 1], [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times/136150924/ 10]|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times/136314643/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 5, 2023}}</ref> Pardee inherited a Chargers unit that ranked 18th out of 28 teams in points allowed per game (20.4) during the regular season,<ref name=norcross_07191981/> and surrendered 24 or more points seven times, including the playoffs.<ref>{{cite news|title=AFC West|date=August 30, 1981|newspaper=Democrat and Chronicle|page=8E|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/democrat-and-chronicle/136309963/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 5, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=1980 San Diego Chargers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees|work=Pro Football Reference|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/sdg/1980.htm|access-date=December 5, 2023}}</ref> However, it also ranked sixth in yards allowed per game (293.2).<ref name=norcross_07191981/> Pardee named four new [[starting lineup|starters]] on defense. Only the cornerbacks remained the same in the [[secondary (football)|secondary]], with Gregor and [[Frank Duncan (American football)|Frank Duncan]] replacing [[Pete Shaw (American football)|Pete Shaw]] and [[Mike Fuller]] as safeties.<ref>{{cite news|first=Ailene|last=Voisin|title=Big Plays, Turnovers Redeem Porous, Inconsistent Defense|date=September 23, 1981|newspaper=The San Diego Union|page=C-1|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-13CF0D80DC98F62D@2444871-13CF0BA1ECAEA71B@32-13CF0BA1ECAEA71B@|url-access=subscription|via=NewsBank|access-date=December 4, 2023}}</ref> With the height and range that Pardee desired,<ref>{{cite news|first=Bill|last=Bisheff|title=New faces dot Chargers' defensive lineup|date=September 3, 1981|newspaper=Evening Tribune|page=C-1|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6CB81C5E443C@NGPA-CASD-185DE08C745390C3@2444851-185DDAE6B446D00D@65-185DDAE6B446D00D@|url-access=subscription|via=NewsBank|access-date=December 6, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first=Jerry|last=Magee|title=Chargers Pass On Old-Timers|date=October 15, 1981|newspaper=The San Diego Union|pages=[https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-13CCBE2EDA8A2EE4@2444893-13CCBDBA2955BB45@39 C-1], [https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-13CCBE2EDA8A2EE4@2444893-13CCB0B56F079C14@41 C-3]|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-13CCBE2EDA8A2EE4@2444893-13CCBDBA2955BB45@39|url-access=subscription|via=NewsBank|access-date=December 6, 2023}}</ref>  Gregor started the first six games at [[free safety]]. The team's second-leading [[tackle (football move)|tackler]] at the time, he was sidelined for the next {{frac|1|1|2}} games by a [[pinched nerve]] in his neck, which hampered him for the rest of the season.<ref name=norcross_08251984/> San Diego's defense was among the NFL's worst, ranked 26th with 390 points allowed (24.4 per game) for the season along with a league-worst 269.4 yards passing per game.<ref>{{cite news|first=John|last=Maffei|title=Chargers have trouble finding defensive help|date=February 25, 1982|newspaper=Times-Advocate|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/136318505/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 6, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=1981 San Diego Chargers Rosters, Stats, Schedule, Team Draftees|work=Pro Football Reference|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/sdg/1981.htm|access-date=December 8, 2023}}</ref> Their defensive backfield was much maligned. The Chargers were again denied a trip to the Super Bowl after losing to [[Cincinnati Bengals|Cincinnati]] in a frigid AFC title game known as the [[Freezer Bowl]].<ref>{{cite news|first=John|last=Maffei|title=Look for many changes in Chargers' 1983 edition|date=August 8, 1982|newspaper=The Times-Advocate|pages=[https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate-chargers-1981-wrap-up/136318887/ D1], [https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/138222180/ D2]|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate-chargers-1981-wrap-up/136318887/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=January 7, 2024}}</ref>

Under new San Diego defensive coordinator [[Tom Bass (American football)|Tom Bass]] in [[1982 San Diego Chargers season|1982]], Gregor moved to strong safety.<ref name=canepa_09161982/> Chargers secondary coach [[Jim Wagstaff]] continued to suggest to Gregor that he curb his hitting intensity to reduce his injury risk. Coryell said that his safety "hits so hard, he maims himself. He's suicidal."<ref>{{cite news|first=Jerry|last=Magee|title=Chargers Seek Protection For 'Hit Man'|date=August 8, 1982|newspaper=The San Diego Union|page=H-3|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-13D1E7C622019A10@2445190-13D19EF68659E180@108-13D19EF68659E180@|via=NewsBank|url-access=subscription|access-date=December 5, 2023}}</ref> In the season opener, Gregor and fellow safety [[Andre Young (American football)|Andre Young]] played a large part in forcing [[Denver Broncos|Denver]] into six turnovers.<ref name=canepa_09161982>{{cite news|first=Nick|last=Canepa|title=Gregor embodies hard-hitting side of Chargers' defense|date=September 16, 1982|newspaper=Evening Tribune|page=E-8|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6CB81C5E443C@NGPA-CASD-185BBA581D9E2A45@2445229-18599F79AE6CF9AB@87-18599F79AE6CF9AB@|via=NewsBank|url-access=subscription|access-date=December 5, 2023}}</ref> In the third game, Gregor dislocated his elbow against the Raiders,<ref name=norcross_08251984/> when he was reaching to strip the ball from a Raiders player and Chargers teammate [[Dewey Selmon]] ran through his arm.<ref name=shaw_09101983>{{cite news|first=Bud|last=Shaw|title=If Charger Bob Gregor Can Remain Healthy...|date=September 10, 1983|newspaper=Evening Tribune|pages=[https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6CB81C5E443C@NGPA-CASD-185E5D592F4EE712@2445588-185A80975BB64BEE@17-185A80975BB64BEE@ B-2], [https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6CB81C5E443C@NGPA-CASD-185E5D592F4EE712@2445588-185DCA9959E62748@22 B-7]|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6CB81C5E443C@NGPA-CASD-185E5D592F4EE712@2445588-185A80975BB64BEE@17-185A80975BB64BEE@|url-access=subscription|via=NewsBank|access-date=December 3, 2023}}</ref> Gregor missed the next five games of the nine-game season, shortened by [[1982 NFL strike|a strike]] that year.<ref name=norcross_08251984/>

In the [[1983 San Diego Chargers season|1983 season]] opener, Gregor was diagnosed with a [[concussion]] in a 41–29 loss to the [[New York Jets]].<ref name=shaw_09101983/><ref>{{cite news|first=Jerry|last=Magee|title=Crowded sideline may have contributed to error|date=September 6, 1983|newspaper=The San Diego Union|page=C-5|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-13D15BE7633CFC16@2445584-13D1572D4A13BF2D@32-13D1572D4A13BF2D@|via=NewsBank|url-access=subscription|access-date=December 5, 2023}}</ref> Reflecting on his history, he called the injuries "frustrating".<ref name=shaw_09101983/> He added, "I've had my share of concussions. But considering the other possibilities, a concussion isn't that bad".<ref name=shaw_09101983/> Gregor started the season's first five games before a knee injury ended his season. The injury occurred against the [[New York Giants]], which he started with his former college teammate [[Ken Greene]] at free safety, their first NFL start together.<ref>{{cite news|first=Jerry|last=Magee|title=Chargers to double-team Giants|date=September 29, 1983|newspaper=The San Diego Union|page=C-1|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-13D0B538093C3B65@2445607-13D0B163C61A2346@38|url-access=subscription|via=NewsBank|access-date=December 6, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=San Diego Chargers at New York Giants – October 2nd, 1983|work=Pro Football Reference|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/198310020nyg.htm|access-date=December 6, 2023}}</ref> The injury was not initially considered to be season-ending, but he eventually underwent two [[arthroscopy|arthroscopic surgeries]].<ref name=norcross_08251984/> After Gregor appeared in just 23 games in three years as a starter,<ref name=ta_08301984/> the Chargers attempted to increase his availability by starting [[Miles McPherson]] in his place in [[1984 San Diego Chargers season|1984]].<ref name=norcross_08251984>{{cite news|first=Don|last=Norcross|title=Bob Gregor: Professional 'patient' hasn't altered his hard-hitting style|date=August 25, 1984|newspaper=Times-Advocate|at=sec. North County Consumer News, p. 19|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/136146371/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 3, 2023}}</ref> Nonetheless, Gregor's season ended after he tore ankle ligaments in week 7 against [[Kansas City Chiefs|Kansas City]] and was placed on injured reserve.<ref>{{cite news|first=Dan|last=Norcross|title=Primary trouble is secondary|date=October 17, 1984|newspaper=Times-Advocate|page=C1|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/136365350/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 7, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Scouting report|date=October 21, 1984|newspaper=Times-Advocate|page=C6|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/136365386/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 7, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Bob Gregor 1984 Game Log|work=Pro Football Reference|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GregBo20/gamelog/1984/|access-date=December 7, 2023}}</ref>

After years of ranking among the worst defenses in the NFL, San Diego decided during the offseason to begin an extensive youth movement. On July 9, 1985, Gregor was among eight veterans, including six on defense, who were released.<ref name=magee_07101985>{{cite news|last=Magee|first=Jerry|title=Chargers cut eight veterans, sign Jackson|date=July 10, 1985|newspaper=San Diego Union|pages=[https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-1739BD9C246A1303@2446257-1739BCBBBB90D891@46 E-1], [https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-1739BD9C246A1303@2446257-1739BCBD9DC97227@52 E-7]|url=https://sandiegouniontribune.newsbank.com/doc/image/v2:136E6A0F0DF56B38@NGPA-CASD-1739BD9C246A1303@2446257-1739BCBBBB90D891@46|url-access=subscription|via=NewsBank|access-date=December 3, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first=Jay|last=Posner|title=Defense boasts new—probably better—look|date=September 5, 1985|newspaper=Times-Advocate|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/times-advocate/136151972/|at=sec. North County Consumer News, p. 10|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|access-date=December 5, 2023}}</ref> [[Jerry Magee]] of ''[[The San Diego Union]]'' wrote that "the slightly built Gregor ... played with a recklessness that was his own undoing."<ref name=magee_07101985/>

==Later life==
After his career in 2012, Gregor joined a concussion-related [[class-action lawsuit]] against the NFL. The lawsuit stated that due to repeated head impacts during his NFL career, "Gregor has experienced cognitive and other difficulties including, but not limited to headaches, dizziness, loss of memory, depression, suicidal thoughts, sleep problems, and neck and cervical arthritis and associated numbness/tingling."<ref>{{cite web|title=IN RE: NATIONAL FOOTBALL LEAGUE PLAYERS' CONCUSSION INJURY LITIGATION|publisher=UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF PENNSYLVANIA|page=12|url=https://media.cleveland.com/science_impact/other/Concussion%20-%20Boyd%20vs.%20NFL.pdf|access-date=December 1, 2023}}</ref> In 2015, a federal judge approved a settlement plan that could potentially cost the league $1 billion in payments to players over 65 years.<ref>{{cite news|title=Judge approves potential $1 billion settlement to resolve NFL concussion lawsuits|date=April 22, 2015|newspaper=USA Today|agency=AP|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2015/04/22/nfl-concussion-lawsuit-settlement-judge-1-billion/26192827/|access-date=December 1, 2023}}</ref>

'''Robert Lester Beemer''' (born May 14, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for the [[Detroit Lions]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Toledo Rockets football|Toledo Rockets]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BeemBo20.htm| title=Bob Beemer Stats |access-date=July 28, 2021 |publisher=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Bob Beemer, DE |url=https://www.nfl.com/players/bob-beemer/ |access-date=July 28, 2021 |work=Nfl.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://utrockets.com/sports/2015/3/17/GEN_20140101192| title=Bob Beemer, Football (1982-1985) |publisher=University of Toledo Athletics.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=V|first=Josh|last2=Jv|first2=Yke {{!}}|date=2019-11-13|title=25 greatest football players of all time from the Jackson area|url=https://www.mlive.com/sports/g66l-2019/11/a7ce5442163448/25-greatest-football-players-of-all-time-from-the-jackson-area.html|access-date=2021-09-03|website=mlive|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.utrockets.com/news/2010/2/26/Bob_Beemer_Football_1982_1985_.aspx|archive-date=2016-06-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160624040229/http://www.utrockets.com/news/2010/2/26/Bob_Beemer_Football_1982_1985_.aspx|title=Bob Beemer Football 1982-1985|publisher=University of Toledo Rockets}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Stine|first=Carl|title=College Football 2011: What One Player Best Embodies Each FBS Team?|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/686325-college-football-what-one-player-best-embodies-each-fbs-team|access-date=2021-09-03|website=Bleacher Report|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Bockmore unsung hero on UT defense|url=https://www.toledoblade.com/sports/ut/2001/11/15/Bockmore-unsung-hero-on-UT-defense/stories/200111150079|access-date=2021-09-03|website=The Blade|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=The Blade {{!}} Toledo's breaking news, sports, and entertainment watchdog|url=https://www.toledoblade.com/|access-date=2021-09-03|website=The Blade|language=en}}</ref>
